We demonstrate the existence of nonlinear traveling waves near the Couette flow in 2D for the Navier-Stokes equation, with these waves approximating solutions to a conservative Hamiltonian system. Specifically, we show that for large values of the rotation parameter $\epsilon$ (with $0 < \epsilon < 1$), there exist traveling waves whose velocities are less than $\epsilon^{\frac{-1}{6}}$. Furthermore, when $\epsilon$ approaches zero, the approximation of solutions to the conservative Hamiltonian system improves significantly. Notably, although it has been long established that these solutions asymptotically converge in some topological space, our work seems to be the first to derive a quantitative error bound for this convergence. 

The approach employed here, building on previous research by Bedrossian et al. in 2017, primarily relies on two distinct aspects: the development of a reference background by Bedrossian et al. and an energy estimate technique, which was initially introduced and applied to the Quasi-Geostrophy equation by Chiron and Gazeau. 

It is worth noting that the nonlinear interaction in the conservative Hamiltonian system is minimal, thereby allowing for the application of a simple energy estimate that helps achieve a strong convergence result. The reference background, which is essential for the energy estimate, is constructed through a process involving local frequency projections and an analysis of the nonlinear interaction in the conservation law. The result of this construction is a point with particularly low nonlinear interaction, thereby simplifying the application of the energy estimate and yielding a quantitative error bound for the convergence. 

The approach of integrating Bedrossian's background and the energy estimate, which was initially introduced and applied to the Quasi-Geostrophy equation by Chiron and Gazeau, appears to provide a versatile method that can be used for a broad range of conservative partial differential equations. On the other hand, the notion of integrating reference backgrounds with high nonlinear interaction and the application of the energy estimate where low nonlinear interaction is preferred seems less feasible. 

The research has several potential future implications and suggests several potential areas of investigation. Firstly, it is conjectured that the upper limit of the velocity in the traveling waves can be further optimized. Secondly, it is suspected that the approximation can be improved indefinitely as long as $\epsilon$ remains positive. Lastly, it is proposed that the result can be extended and applied to scenarios with external forces that are small in magnitude.

The 2020 SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has become the deadliest in global history, with South Africa being among the hardest hit countries. This study analyzed Google trends data alongside energy consumption and search query data from various sources to evaluate their effectiveness as alternative indicators of the pandemic's progression. The findings reveal a striking resemblance between these data sources and officially reported COVID-19 case numbers, demonstrating their utility in forecasting the outbreak's evolution. Moreover, incorporating machine learning techniques improved the forecasting accuracy, suggesting their potential to further enhance the modeling process. By leveraging these accessible data sources and machine learning methods, policymakers can make more informed decisions, even in scenarios where limited data is available and real-time COVID-19 updates are delayed. The proposed framework boasts adaptive capabilities, enabling it to be easily adapted and applied to other countries with minimal modifications. Furthermore, the study's findings underscore the profound impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions on combating the pandemic, as well as the societal implications of citizens' behavior and awareness levels. The proposed framework is specifically tailored to address the unique challenges faced by developing countries like South Africa and can be potentially applied to other countries with similar constraints. A significant area of study within additive combinatorics is Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture, a key component of which involves the analysis of sum sets within a certain range. This article enhances the existing conclusions of 3k-4 conjecture by providing an optimized upper limit for the size of a sum set within a specified range. Our findings not only expand upon the existing work of Planchel and Zarichnyi but also yield a more streamlined proof with additional structural implications. Additionally, our research leads to the discovery of two new Freiman's type 2 conjectures, along with their respective full solutions. Finally, our work facilitates the derivation of an optimal Freiman's 4k-1 conjecture with a full proof.

A graph-based neural network approach called dynamic graph message passing network has previously been employed in computer vision, however its potential in learning object representations is largely unexplored. We present a neuro-symbolic model that incorporates a dynamic graph message passing network to learn an object's visual features and identify its inherent characteristics. The temporal evolution of an object's attributes is represented as a dynamic graph with nodes corresponding to time stamps. Edges are divided into two categories: short-range edges that facilitate message exchange between nearby time stamps and long-range edges that allow nodes to access distant information. The central node performs a task-specific analysis of the object's features. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our model on multiple visual identification tasks and showcase its ability to learn dynamic graphs that resemble real-world object characteristics. The proposed model outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on multiple visual identification tasks and achieves this through well-designed dynamic graphs that effectively capture an object's features. The model's source code will be publicly available.

A compact muon collider is suggested as a cutting-edge high-energy particle collider. This concept is presented as a feasible successor to the LHC and Higgs factory ideas. A muon collider would serve several purposes, including examining the Compton shoulder of the Z-boson and studying the Higgs boson with enhanced precision, in addition to exploring new physics beyond the Standard Model. However, the muon collider's technical challenges are substantial and have not yet been thoroughly addressed. A comprehensive study by an APPC working group has identified and compared the collider's design options and has highlighted the key obstacles to implementation. These obstacles include establishing a reliable muon accelerator and a high-intensity muon accelerator as a precursor to the collider, as well as introducing a new generation of superconducting magnets and radio-frequency systems, and developing a high-brightness muon source with a high-duty cycle. Furthermore, the working group has emphasized the necessity of addressing research and development hurdles, such as cooling schemes, that might hinder construction. Ultimately, the report presents a future roadmap for R&D endeavors required to make a practical muon collider a reality. The estimate suggests that in order to avoid the PBH-induced cosmological constraints on dark matter, the ratio of relevant quantum fluctuations to thermal fluctuations must be lower than 10^(-3). The stringent limit originates from the high rate at which black holes of any mass undergo annihilation in the present-day cosmic background radiation. This paper introduces the Virtual Safe Framework, a novel, five-stage pipeline-based processor architecture that enhances and simplifies the execution of complex programs on programmable GPUs over TFHE encryption. The VSF's innovative design tackles two key challenges: bypassing memory access issues and addressing the requirement for a fixed, predetermined execution path. The VSF's efficiency was evaluated through performance testing on a GPU, yielding notable gains of 2.97x and 20.13x in execution speed and memory efficiency, respectively, when compared to the current state-of-the-art CuckooHash-based approach under identical, whole-program evaluation conditions. Furthermore, the study successfully demonstrated the successful execution of 12 real-world programs utilizing the VSF, encompassing 4 encryption-based, 4 hashing-based applications, along with 4 benchmark tools. The research also involved an in-depth examination of program performance, revealing that program-specific performance could be improved by customizing the VSF to fulfill distinct requirements. The proposed framework's memory-efficient and execution-speed enhancements offer promising potential for mainstream encryption usage in hardware and software systems. The research provides an open-source VSF implementation for general access, along with the accompanying source code posted on GitHub. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on certain graph classes, but required an exponential number of sub-problems to solve instances.

A more efficient PTAS was later developed by Khanna, et al., which ran in O(n^(1-ε))/poly time, but was only applicable to classes with very restricted structure.

A better PTAS was developed for the Minimum Vertex Cover problem on $k$-degenerate graphs, which ran in O(n/m)/poly time.

This research presents a new efficient PTAS for a broader class of weighted CSPs that have a unique and consistent structure, even when the constraints are complex and not easily computable.

The developed algorithm runs in O(n/m)(1+1/(2alpha^m)) time, where alpha is a constant greater than 1, making it significantly faster than previous PTAS on similar problems, which ran in O(n^1-epsilon)/poly time. 

A particular case of this problem is Minimum Vertex Cover on k-degenerate graphs, for which the developed algorithm runs in O(n^1-epsilon)/poly time, improving the previous most efficient result by running in O(n/m)/poly time when m is an upper bound for n. 

New techniques are proposed to design this efficient PTAS, including:

* A general method for the Maximum Independent Set problem, which uses constrained programming and can be applied to classes of graphs with limited connectivity and any number of constraints.

* A new efficient algorithm for the Minimum Vertex Cover problem, which uses a constrained programming approach and can handle a limited number of constraints with complex relationships.

* New efficient algorithms for the Maximum Independent Set and Minimum Vertex Cover problems, which use a novel technique that constrains the structure of the graph, allowing for a more efficient search for solutions.

In a 1983 paper by Fredman and Horowitz, it was demonstrated that in a RAM model with bit operations, the cost of executing a shift by one bit is equivalent to two addition operations. Based on this finding, it can be shown that multiplying two integers by two involves the same computational expense as adding those integers, which in turn can be performed in $O(\log n)$ operations if the RAM model relies on addition. If the input integers in the RAM are represented as binary sequences rather than implicit numbers, it is possible to achieve a constant time cost for a range of integer operations including those involving one-bit shifts, multiplying by two, identifying the most significant bit, and taking the square root (modulo some small constant). While these operations can be executed in constant time when the input integers are represented as binary sequences, this advantage is lost if the integers are represented as explicit numbers. It is unknown whether the same advantage can be attained when the input integers are represented as explicit numbers. Furthermore, it is unknown whether the same advantage can be attained for a broader class of operations including identifying the most significant bit and taking the square root. These questions are left unresolved for future investigation. The proposed approach is a methodology for evaluating whether a given sequence of operations can be executed in constant time based on two key conditions being met: (i) all operations involve the same argument, and (ii) each operation is equivalent to the previous one modified by a specific transformation. If both conditions are met, it is demonstrated that the sequence can be executed in constant time based on an analysis of the maximum depth of a binary tree with a specific number of nodes, where each node represents an operation. If the input integers are represented as binary sequences, it is demonstrated that a sequence of operations including identifying the most significant bit and taking the square root can be executed in constant time. Recently, a novel application of differential forms has been successful in expressing a variety of network-derived geometric constructs, including Zonoids, Radon transforms, and Feynman integrals. However, the traditional approach of classical differential forms falls short in capturing the genuine topology of these constructs. In contrast, a newly introduced concept known as 'differential shape' effectively addresses this shortcoming by combining invariant differential forms with a weight function. In this paper, we further develop the underlying algebraic framework of differential shapes, enabling us to study the topological properties of geometric constructs using techniques like de Rham cohomology. By achieving a full understanding of the topological characteristics, we are able to apply invariant integration to shape-derived differential forms, thereby enabling a straightforward computation of key network Zonoid characteristics such as the Hodge vector and orientability. Moreover, our findings reveal a profound connection between scattering amplitudes and geometric constructs, where the differential shape paradigm serves as a unified framework for describing both real and virtual scattering amplitudes. As such, this paper presents a groundbreaking, universally applicable approach to addressing both on-shell and off-shell Feynman integrals within a single mathematical framework. Furthermore, our work identifies a critical relationship between the rationality of correlation functions and the algebraic geometry of the associated shapes. Ultimately, this paper concludes by highlighting the vast potential of the differential shape program to explore various applications at the interface of quantum field theory and geometric topology. The aim of this research was to examine how these characteristics influence learning in a recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for object classification. An experiment was conducted involving two RNNs trained on the same dataset, with one network (multi-feature) trained to process multiple object characteristics and another network (single-feature) trained to process a single attribute while ignoring the others. An additional experiment involved replacing the multi-feature network with a ensemble of single-feature networks, each trained on a different attribute. The results of these experiments indicated that the characteristics of objects are exploited by the RNNs through sectorisation of the input space and highlighted the capacity of RNNs to directly engage with task-relevant data features without necessarily undergoing implicit segmentation. Additionally, it was found that each attribute contributes uniquely and independently to the classification process. The findings of this study may influence future training protocols of RNNs and highlight the potential of multi-feature and ensemble-based training methods for object classification tasks. In a non-Hermitian system with a topological edge, we investigate how interactions influence the underlying non-Hermiticity and topological characteristics. Our findings indicate that weak interactions can lead to an expansion of the region where non-Hermiticity dominates and thus diminish the topological edge. Altered areas in hyperspectral images can be identified but detecting changes is a major challenge, particularly when the extent of alteration is minimal. Most current methods fail to recognize unsupervised alterations due to their reliance on approximation and limited coverage. In this study, a novel approach called Feature Integration Deep Conversion Autoencoders (FIDCAE) is presented, leveraging a combination of local and global features captured by a pair of deep convolutional autoencoders trained on unsupervised alteration detection. A novel feature integration strategy is introduced to combine the local and global features at various scales, enabling the recognition of alterations extending beyond a single pixel. In comparison to existing methods such as PCA, AutoPD, and LocalPD, the proposed FIDCAE achieved the best performance on two real-world hyperspectral image datasets by successfully identifying alterations extending beyond a single pixel. The source code for FIDCAE is available at https://github.com/JiaWang007/FeatureIntegrationDeepConvolutionalAutoencoders. Additionally, the two hyperspectral image datasets used in this study can be accessed at https://github.com/JiaWang007/TwoRealWorldHSPIs. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in detecting alterations, particularly those that are slight. The proposed FIDCAE was successfully applied to two real-world hyperspectral images, revealing its potential for a variety of practical uses, such as monitoring land use, detecting alterations, and agricultural management. FIDCAE can potentially be adapted for detecting alterations in other image modalities. Lastly, the proposed FIDCAE can serve as a baseline for future studies on alteration detection. It may also be utilized as a starting point for future research due to its simple structure and the generalizability of its approach, which can be applied to other image modalities. In particular, the feature integration strategy integrated into FIDCAE could be applied to other autoencoder-based methods to enhance their performance. FIDCAE also offers a possible explanation for the success of deep convolutional autoencoders in feature extraction tasks by revealing the significance of local features at various scales. Furthermore, the proposed FIDCAE provides a possible solution to the long-standing feature selection problem by demonstrating that combining local and global features can lead to better performance, which may not be the case for other supervised or unsupervised methods. We aim to develop an automated system to create resilient control systems using decision theory's robust optimal policy. The robust optimal policy serves as a reliable control system in the face of uncertain systems and adversaries. Traditional approaches for finding this policy involve solving a mathematical model, but this requires precise knowledge of the adversary's actions, which can be difficult to obtain. Our system, however, allows for discovering a resilient control system through observation of the adversary's actions over time. The algorithm generates controllers that approximate the robust optimal policy and adapts to newly discovered adversary behavior. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm in developing resilient controllers for a practical industrial setting. The algorithm is valued for its ability to produce a responsive controller that adapts to emerging patterns of adversary behavior. Although not solely focused on discovering the robust optimal policy, our algorithm is capable of directing attention towards high-value regions of the robust optimal policy's state-space, particularly those that can provide robust performance in the long term. The algorithm is positioned such that it is always better off following the robust optimal policy than any alternative strategy. The design of our algorithm is grounded in the idea that, through the exploration of the robust optimal policy's state-space, it is possible to gain a more accurate understanding of the adversary's behavior, thereby allowing the algorithm to adapt and improve over time. The algorithm's approach to exploration is centered on the premise that future instances of the state-space are expected to resemble past instances, and thus, it prioritizes visiting states that are expected to occur frequently in the future. The algorithm's decision-making process is guided by the perception that, through the discovery of a robust control strategy, it is possible to achieve more sustained success in the long term. The effectiveness of our algorithm is demonstrated through both theoretical validation and experimental results. The performance of the algorithm is evaluated in a practical industrial setting and compared against an alternative method that is designed to test its underlying assumption that the discovery of a robust control strategy is associated with improved performance. The results of these experiments provide strong evidence that the algorithm is a robust control strategy is associated with improved performance. The algorithm's ability to prioritize visiting states that are expected to occur frequently in the future is a key component of its decision-making process, and it is this ability that allows the algorithm to direct attention towards high-value regions of the robust optimal policy's state-space. The algorithm's reliance on frequentist estimates is another important aspect of its decision-making process, and it is this reliance that provides strong evidence that the discovery of a robust control strategy is associated with improved performance.

We introduce a novel framework, referred to as the PAV framework, for developing novel schemes in encoded caching and decentralized computing. The framework provides a clear approach to establish the efficiency and a crucial benchmark, the efficiency limit, for any scheme within its domain. Through the PAV framework, we derive a systematic method for constructing cache and error correction codes that are specifically designed to optimize performance in encoded caching schemes and establish the existence of an efficiently constructible code that achieves the efficiency limit. This leads to a seamless extension to decentralized computing schemes, allowing us to obtain the best achievable performance and an easily buildable code that approaches it. Furthermore, we present a practical code construction method for both caching and decentralized computing systems of any size, enabling these codes to be efficiently used in any scheme size. Our experimental results confirm that the PAV framework consistently produces performance that closely matches the efficiency limit across a range of relevant system sizes. Moreover, the framework enables the creation of PAV-efficient codes that offer superior performance compared to existing benchmark codes in both caching and decentralized computing. The framework's tools enable seamless adaptation to any scheme variant, as illustrated by our extension of the efficiency limit formula to a recently proposed dual variant of decentralized computing. This extension leads to a significant performance gain over the standard PAV framework. Finally, we investigate the connection between efficiency and entropy in both caching and decentralized computing, revealing that there is no inherent correlation between these two concepts based on our framework's fundamental properties. However, for any scheme, its entropy does impose a natural performance ceiling. The study concludes with our discovery that several recently proposed codes are indeed optimal, while many notable codes are suboptimal. Conversely, the PAV framework catalyzes the creation of yet-unseen, efficient code families that can rival and even surpass existing benchmark codes. The study presents a comprehensive performance evaluation of the proposed PAV framework through a range of numerical examples that showcase its versatility and adaptability to various coding problems, including accumulation, product, and matrix-based coding. A novel algorithm, called SIGNO, is introduced to identify the non-degenerate components of a polynomial system. SIGNO initially derives signature-based non-degenerate components from a given system using a parameter-dependent analysis. It then implements two techniques: an induction method for overall non-degeneracy assessment and a certification procedure for independently validating the results. Furthermore, SIGNO's methods are demonstrated to be computationally efficient with optimal complexity. Finally, a comprehensive set of examples is provided to showcase the algorithm's efficacy in various applications. It is noteworthy that SIGNO has successfully determined non-degeneracy for polynomial systems of arity 9 or lower in all relevant cases. The algorithm has been openly disseminated at https://git.io/signo. Additionally, a comprehensive database of computed non-degeneracy values is accessible at https://algo-line.gitlab.io/signo. The predictions take into account nuclear-physics effects in the interactions and are compared to the measurements at the same energy taken at the RHIC, as part of the PHENIX collaboration. A longstanding problem posed by Turan in 1941 involves determining whether there are exact coverings of a certain $n$-dimensional vector space with subsets of size $e$, where each subset covers all but at most $\delta n$ coordinates. We nearly resolve this issue by showing that for large enough $n$, no such covering exists with $e < (1 - \omega(\sqrt{n/e}))e$. This result is related to a long-standing conjecture put forth by Frankl and Pach in 1985, which suggests that no covering with at most two elements exists for $n$-dimensional vector spaces. Our work also addresses a related issue known as the tetrahedron problem, which has been solved for binary vector spaces by Friedgut, Kahn, and Wigderson in 1999. We successfully generalize this problem in the $\ell_2$-metric by showing that for large enough $n$, no covering with at most three elements exists that covers all but at most $\delta n$ coordinates for any $\delta < 1/3.5. This new constant is very close to the known upper limit of $\delta \approx 0.853$. This result is notable as it is the first time a generalization of the tetrahedron problem has been proven for a specific and commonly used metric. Furthermore, our findings imply that no covering with at most four elements exists that covers all but at most $n/3$ coordinates. This proof is independent of the Franklin-Pach conjecture and implies that no covering with at most two elements exists that covers all but at most $n/3$ coordinates, providing further evidence for this conjecture. We combine Fourier analysis and measure theory to establish these results and provide a new approach for addressing the Turan problem. We also evaluate the feasibility and efficiency of the proposed algorithm at resolving the problem. We successfully tested this algorithm on vectors of up to dimension 128, which are well within the realm of the medium-scale ($n\sim 10^4$) to large-scale ($n\sim 10^6$) range that our approach is designed for. We also evaluate the suitability of the algorithm for resolving the problem in the $\ell_2$-metric by covering all but at most $n/3$ coordinates, which is a scale that is also well within the realm of the medium-scale ($n\sim 10^6$) to large-scale ($n\sim 10^6$) range

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their simplicity, flexibility, and minimal weight. However, accurately modeling and controlling soft grippers proves to be challenging due to their deformable nature. Soft grippers can be effectively modeled using a simplified representation of physical systems, which relies on linear parameter-varying (LPV) parameters for their representation. However, determining these LPV parameters is a complex task. This research employs the Koopman operator theory to solve this problem by utilizing the gripper's images through time and utilizing machine learning tools for their identification. The proposed method achieves a successful practical implementation in simulations and real-world tests on a three-fingered soft gripper. The results of this research open up the possibility of remotely controlling and regulating the movement of soft and flexible robotic arms. One significant issue with gradient descent is developing algorithms that efficiently generalize across various underlying functions. The natural gradient descent, which incorporates the curvature of the function via its Hessian, represents a notable generalization solution. However, this method's scalability is limited by its quadratic computational and memory complexities. The natural gradient in its original form only addresses the direction of the gradient, overlooking important discerning differences between functions. In this study, we develop a new generalization approach called the organic gradient, which records the relative differences between functions and utilizes them to recognize distinctive characteristics. A key advantage of the organic gradient is its applicability to a broad range of functions without explicit reconstruction of their underlying structures. The computational complexity of our method is linear and memory-complexity is constant, making it highly scalable and adaptable to diverse functions. Our experiments, conducted across multiple synthetic and real-world environments, demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the organic gradient descent algorithm. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical application of our method in the organic evolution of neural networks. The developed framework and associated source code are accessible via https://github.org/bassuaman/OGD. Natural language statements can effectively serve as a comprehensive description of a scenario, encompassing all relevant details. This description can be utilized in reinforcement learning to establish a clear objective and gauge performance. While text-based descriptions may initially seem straightforward, they exhibit a range of complexities, including ambiguous statements, partial information, and numerous possible interpretation methods. Despite these challenges, numerous research studies have employed natural language descriptions in reinforcement learning contexts. This document presents a concise summary of existing research methodologies centered on natural language state descriptions, focusing on text-based representations and their respective advantages and drawbacks. Additionally, we introduce the NLSD benchmark, comprising three challenging domains that encompass partial information, explicit objectives, and descriptions characterized by ambiguity, as well as a unified set of evaluation metrics designed to assess the efficacy of natural language state descriptions in reinforcement learning. This benchmark serves to facilitate comparative research across diverse approaches to natural language state descriptions. We anticipate that future research will yield improved natural language state descriptions, ultimately leading to enhanced performance in reinforcement learning applications. The observation of gravitational waves from merging black holes by the LIGO and VIRGO Collaborations has enabled researchers to test general relativity in the late stages of a binary's evolution, but the precise memory of gravitational waves from the late stages remains largely unknown. Recent findings suggest that the late-time memory could be substantial enough to create a background of gravitational waves throughout the entire universe. Estimating the intensity of this background requires calculating the rate at which binary black hole mergers produce gravitational waves with significant memory, a phenomenon that is largely unpredictable given the current uncertainty in late-stage binary evolution models. A novel approach involves utilizing Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to generate a vast number of random binary black hole merger events and incorporating these events into a gravitational wave background analysis. The technique, known as the Gravitational Wave Backdrop Simulator, is shown to be an effective tool for calculating the intensity of the gravitational wave background and for identifying observational probes that are most sensitive to the details of binary evolution, such as the gravitational wave delay signal. Furthermore, the Gravitational Wave Backdrop Simulator can also be used to generate realistic ringdown signals from accreting black holes, a feature that is demonstrated in the accompanying paper. The module also includes additional functionality to analyze the events, as well as a graphical interface based on PyGWCode that allows for the visualization of binary black hole mergers in the GW-skymap format. The extensive collaborative resource, Wikipedia, relies on community edits to maintain its high standards. However, the process also permits malicious actors to infiltrate and propagate low-quality content, particularly through the "Articles for Deletion" process. Previous research aimed to identify patterns in Wikipedia edits to categorize content as high or low quality, which could aid in automatically tagging suspicious articles. Leveraging pattern-based analysis from existing studies, this research focuses on articles marked for deletion on German Wikipedia, examining two types of patterns: (1) textual similarities and (2) temporal relationships between edits. Then, it applies a binary classification model to determine if these patterns are indicative of low-quality tags. Finally, a predictive model is developed to automatically assign low-quality tags based on detected patterns. Results show that both patterns and the predictive model significantly correlate with low-quality tags on articles marked for deletion, as well as unmarked articles, indicating a significant correlation between editing patterns and low-quality content. As AI systems continue to scale, their trustworthiness persists as a significant challenge. The underlying issue is that most current robustness approaches rely on specific architectural assumptions and often require substantial insight into the underlying model. This may not be a major concern when working with basic neural networks, but it becomes a serious limitation when dealing with more complex models such as transfer learning setups, where large amounts of knowledge are transferred from one model to another. 

In this paper, we introduce a black-box framework called Decision-Based Black-Box (D3) that builds on existing black-box methods but demands minimal to no information about the target model. The D3 approach successfully tackles the knowledge transfer problem without requiring any explicit labels or internal model details. This transfer model is trained in a zero-shot manner, implying that no data is required for the new domain as long as it shares a similar label structure with the source domain. 

We test our proposed method using the robustness assessment framework and four real-world image classification datasets, comparing its performance to two prominent black-box methods, Adversarial Training and Ensemble DeepPoly. The results indicate that D3 consistently outperforms these methods across various evaluation metrics and domains. This study focuses on developing efficient Co-Observation learning strategies for Multi-Agent systems. Co-Observation learning enables agents to learn from each other through mutual interaction, without requiring separate demonstrations. We analyze two key aspects: (i) the impact of opponents on learning and (ii) the transfer of skills between opposing agents. Our research reveals that the transfer of skills occurs more easily when opposing agents engage in similar observations. To maximize this transfer, we propose a novel strategy that encourages agents to collaborate and share observations. The proposed approach performs better than existing methods in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning environments. The results of our experiments demonstrate that shared observations accelerates the learning process and improve the overall performance of the agents. Furthermore, our findings suggest that opposing agents who collaborate and observe similarly can acquire similar skills more efficiently. Our research introduces an innovative tool called ShapePipe, a cutting-edge shape assessment pipeline that utilizes the NGmix model to generate precise galaxy profiles. This tool not only enhances the accuracy of galaxy shape measurements but also facilitates a wide range of scientific research, including weak lensing studies. We successfully applied ShapePipe to the 450,000 galaxies in the UNIONS/CFIS data and achieved a mean critical 50% radius of 0.832 arcseconds for the sample. This demonthored release includes the data used in this study, allowing for replication and further exploration. Our research reveals a 0.998 correlation between ShapePipe and the established LEGACYPipe2 profile catalog, and demonstrates that ShapePipe achieves a 6% improvement in comparison to the widely used SCP-NSCF pipeline. Furthermore, our analysis of the data indicates the presence of a cosmological constant and a mean redshift of 0.62, which was obtained through a 2% accurate weak lensing tomography. This research also shows that ShapePipe's SCALAPRO deployment leads to significant speed and memory savings when compared to other multi-GPU and CPU implementations. Ultimately, this tool and its associated data cater to a variety of scientific research, including but not limited to, cosmological constant and galaxy evolution studies. The key characteristic of BKT transitions is the spontaneous emergence of topological long-range order due to the condensation of two-dimensional vortices. The conventional BKT transitions are observed in easy-axis Heisenberg models when the flare of the rotational symmetry increases with temperature, and this behavior is analogous to $\theta_D$ deformation in Dirac fermions. Moreover, we have discovered that the easy-plane $\mathbb{Z}_3$ BKT transitions can be transformed into easy-axis $\mathbb{Z}_3$ BKT transitions through a field adjustment. The obtained results provide a significant breakthrough in the field and may facilitate further investigations into topological transitions in spin systems. Additionally, we propose that the $\theta_D$-driven $\mathbb{Z}_3$ BKT transition can serve as a $\theta$-emergent degeneracy in magnetization, and this can be tested in the current experiment by adjusting the external field. The obtained results may have significant implications in the field due to these connections. Therefore, the achieved magnetization degeneracy can serve as a novel diagnostic tool for the topological transitions in spin systems. Over the course of ten nights, four $K$2 plates were observed, covering approximately 232.8 square degrees in the Cygnus-Xy Cygnus region. Through an activity detection program, 0.53 activity indices per degree were identified. Data showed that variable objects accounted for roughly 41% of all observed stars, with a dense pattern of periodic variables, primarily associated with DDRK (Deselection by Removal of Known) stars. These variables accounted for about 27% of all observed stars within specific $g$-$K$2 color ranges. Following up on multiple variable stars using the ZTF, it was discovered that as many as 50% of these activity-bearing stars exhibited non-Periodic, constant or less than 10-day variability. In computer science, random number generation is a fundamental process encompassing a wide range of statistical distributions. The most frequently employed method involves the central limit theorem, which generates Gaussian-distributed numbers, often obtained by summing internal states of digital circuits such as counters or shift registers. However, this approach has drawbacks due to the need for additional calculations, which can slow systems down and limit their energy efficiency. A novel, compact technique proposed in this paper generates truly random digits by under-scaling the supply voltage to SRAM cells. This method exploits the statistical distribution of SRAM cell read failures, which can be accurately modeled and provide up to 32 bits of randomness. By harnessing the natural under-scaling events of SRAM memory, the designers can obtain high-quality random numbers with extremely low computational overhead, even as low as 0.0006 $\mu J$. This random number generator can be implemented at a very early stage in the design process with a minimal area cost of less than 5 square micrometers and can easily be adapted to different memory technologies. Its reliability under real-world failures has been validated through extensive testing of 180 nm and 32 nm technology test chips. Furthermore, the generators have passed the NIST standards for random number generation, which includes tests for over 100 billion random digits. This random number generator holds the potential for significantly increasing the energy efficiency of random number-based applications by eliminating costly multiplication operations and enabling the deployment of the generators in harsh environments with reduced risk of failure. The TuRaN tool has been used to replace the PRNG units in latency-sensitive neural network models, resulting in a substantial reduction in latency and energy consumption. Variations in this design were explored, particularly with respect to the middle region, utilizing a conjugated bridge instead. Using a combination of density functional and non-equilibrium electronic transport theories, properties of the designed molecules have been analyzed and their ability to act as single-electron resistive single-electron transistors has been assessed. Our results validate the feasibility of these molecules as efficient single-electron resistive single-electron transistors with considerable current amplification capabilities and stable single charge storage. Moreover, modifying the end groups has been shown to influence these properties. Finally, an adjustable threshold voltage for single-electron switching can be achieved by adjusting the length of the conjugated backbone and the conjugated bridge, respectively. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for developing novel, single-electron-based nonvolatile memory and logic circuit technologies utilizing conjugated backbone-based monomolecular wires. Researchers have used scanning tunneling microscopy to study the variations in spin and orbit from the bulk to the sub-ensemble levels of electroactive transition metal oxides. They found significant spin-orbit variations in oxygen sub-ensembles, but their existence depends on the type of bond between the oxygen and the transition metal. This leads to two distinct behaviors. Crystalline oxides with covalent bonding exhibit gradual spin and orbit variations, whereas those with ionic bonding exhibit sudden changes. These coefficients are Wilson coefficients that significantly influence $b\to s$ transitions and are expected to be directly inferable from $B$-factory data in the near future. We demonstrate that with minimal theoretical precision over a wide Wilson coefficient range, its associated uncertainty can be lowered to a few $10^{-3}$ in a few months of data integration from $B$-factory data, an improvement of which a part can be attributed to correlations with other coefficients. This is feasible due to the vast amount of $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ events that can be handled, unlike in the case of $B^0\to K^0\mu^+\mu^-$ decays where a large number of events leads to equivalent results but requires more complicated analysis. We apply this approach to a known economic model of intergenerational mobility and find that a policy aiming to boost economic mobility may actually decrease it, particularly for higher-social-class groups. The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.

This study proposes a novel coding technique known as degree-degree linked low-density parity-check (DD-LDPC) codes, which can be applied in binary erasure channels. The proposed DD-LDPC code construction method creates a sparsity pattern in the parity-check matrix, where each element's existence is determined by a link between two nodes with specified degrees. This structure allows for a relationship between the degrees of the elements in the parity-check matrix and the erasure probabilities in binary erasure channels. As such, this paper also proposes a method for calculating the minimum degrees required for error-free transmission in such channels. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DD-LDPC code construction method and the erasure probability model. Additionally, it is shown that DD-LDPC codes can offer superior performance compared to conventional LDPC codes. Furthermore, it is observed that DD-LDPC codes can achieve the maximum throughput on binary erasure channels when certain degree sequences are used. This study also proposes a method for jointly designing DD-LDPC codes and variable-length error-control codes to achieve the maximum throughput on binary erasure channels. Numerical examples are provided to verify the superiority of this design method over traditional LDPC codes. Key metrics such as the average node failure rate, the packet failure rate, and the throughput are examined and shown to be improved upon. This design is further observed to be applicable to complex binary erasure channels as well. Lastly, it is confirmed that DD-LDPC codes can be employed in binary erasure channels with erasure probabilities varying across different nodes. This is proven through numerical examples and associated observations. Several potential research areas are identified and suggested for future exploration. Firstly, developing a standardized method for calculating the erasure probabilities in binary erasure channels is a promising area of research. Secondly, developing a method for determining the optimal degrees for error-free transmission in binary erasure channels is another potential research area. Finally, developing a method for jointly designing DD-LDPC codes and variable-length error-control codes to achieve the maximum throughput on general channels is also a promising area of research. This study presents a novel approach known as degree-degree linked low-density parity-check (DD-LDPC) codes for transmitting information over binary erasure channels. Notably, DD-LDPC codes can achieve the maximum throughput on binary erasure channels when specific degree sequences are used. This study also proposes a method for jointly designing DD-LDPC codes and variable-length error-control codes to achieve the maximum throughput on binary erasure channels

Advanced vehicle control systems can trigger unintended consequences, such as lane departure or loss of traction, if the driver is not promptly informed of potential hazards. Vehicle manufacturers are mandated by government regulations to establish safety guidelines for the activation and deactivation of electronic control systems to avert severe accidents. These regulations stimulate the development of the Safety Assessment Tool (SAT), which can evaluate the safety of vehicle designs through numerical simulation. SAT utilizes the Safety Filter Module (SFM) to determine when vehicle subsystems require activation or deactivation based on the vehicle's operational state. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to improving SFM's reliability by enhancing its safety evaluation process. Specifically, we incorporate System Level Synthesis (SLS) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) techniques to refine SFM's performance. Using the widely used Double Lane Change test as a benchmark, we demonstrate that our modified SFM generates more precise and vehicle-specific activation and deactivation timelines, compared to the standard method, thereby minimizing unused and potentially hazardous system activations. These results facilitate the optimization of safety activation patterns that balance vehicle performance and safety concerns. Ultimately, this innovation enables the creation of customized safety protocols for unique vehicle designs and diverse safety specifications. While large-scale pretraining has significantly enhanced the performance of natural language processing tasks, a recent trend has shown that certain models can learn in-context with minimal fine-tuning.  Despite numerous studies on this phenomenon, the underlying effects of pretraining datasets on in-context learning are still not well understood.  To gain more insight, we conducted an in-depth examination of the influence of pretraining datasets on the in-context learning capabilities of a very large language model.  Our analysis of six diverse datasets revealed that the model can effectively adapt to in-context prompts with high performance when pre-trained on datasets with robust semantic context.  Our empirical findings indicate that datasets with such semantic context also facilitate more efficient zero-shot learning on novel tasks.  Importantly, our research includes an empirical observation regarding the relationship between semantic context and the distribution of word frequencies, which may provide a potential key to unlocking in-context learning capabilities.  Ultimately, our study sheds more light on the fundamental question of which pretraining datasets enable a model to learn in-context.  The source code for our project is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jacyAI/in-context-learning and the pre-trained model used in our research is hosted on huggingface.com.

Galaxy groups and clusters serve as the best real-world examples for studying how radio galaxies maintain their energy across vast distances. Their own radiative cooling is, however, insufficient to sustain the power they emit, leading to the emergence of hot plasma from internal heat sources, such as star formations and supernovae explosions. We now examine the impact of radiative cooling on the intergalactic medium in galaxy groups using advanced numerical simulations, focusing on the effects of magnetic fields and thermal conduction. We discover that within a 1 million degree temperature range, a steady balance is reached between radiative cooling and thermal conduction, while at higher and lower temperatures, a complex and unstable equilibrium exists. This equilibrium is particularly affected by the orientation of external magnetic fields and the strength of thermal conduction, ultimately determining the plasma's overall density and the rate at which plasma cools. As a result, the intracluster medium's overall density and the rate at which it cools are both increased when either magnetic fields or thermal conduction cease to operate, leading to extended sound voyages in their absence. We further discover that the absence of magnetic fields causes a significant decrease in the efficiency of radio galaxies to maintain their energy across vast distances, while the absence of thermal conduction leads to a significant drop in the plasma's overall energy across vast distances. This research sheds light on the complex and unstable equilibrium of the intracluster medium and highlights the interconnected role of cooling, magnetic fields, and thermal conduction in maintaining the power dynamics of galaxy groups and clusters. We therefore propose that the phenomenon of quiescent cold gas in these structures should be reevaluated, taking into account the dynamic equilibrium between cooling and conduction that exists within their vast expanses. This research explores the feasibility of synthesizing speech without prior knowledge of language or phonology, but requires knowledge of the underlying units of speech. It investigates Acoustic Phonology Units (APUs) as a means of extracting the building blocks of language, and demonstrates that they can be used to create natural-sounding speech. The APU-based approach is data-efficient and can be applied to languages with limited resources. A limitation of this technique is that it is restricted to languages with phonology similar to English, or languages with phonology greatly differing from English, provided that the underlying phonology can be reasonably inferred. The effectiveness of this method is shown through both subjective and objective evaluations. Specifically, mean opinion scores for the synthesized speech suggest high quality, and mean absolute errors for the duration of phonology units indicate low average duration deviations. Notably, while the synthesized speech scored lowest in subjective metrics when compared to other state-of-the-art approaches, it performed comparably or better in objective metrics. A possible explanation for this observation is that the current approach places less emphasis on learning language-specific units. Future work will focus on developing methods for automatically defining the phonology of unseen languages. Additionally, the presentation discusses potential solutions to scaling the current approach to languages with extensive training data. Finally, the overall feasibility and potential of the zero resource speech synthesis task is assessed. It is concluded that speech synthesis without language-specific training can be achieved given access to the underlying phonology, but speech translation remains a more feasible pursuit. A open-source implementation of the proposed method is available at https://github.com/melbouj/zero-resource-speech-synthesis. It includes a tool for extracting Acoustic Phonology Units from a given corpus, as well as a system for synthesizing speech based on these units. The project also offers a simple and efficient approach to extracting the Acoustic Phonology Units, and defines the phonology of several languages. Furthermore, a leading benchmark for evaluating the quality of speech synthesized without language-specific training is provided, and can be utilized by other researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of their methods. The tool can be accessed at https://github.com/melbouj/zero-resource-speech-synthesis/tree/main/benchmark. It shows that the collection of possible quantum states is a comprehensive set with a singular characteristic - any attempt to create a valid state through probabilistic conversion will inevitably fail if the desired state is not achievable without uncertainty. In essence, we have identified a fundamental, non-trivial limitation on the conversion of quantum states. The underlying logic of our finding revolves around a basic yet profound truth about the conversion of mixed states, which has far-reaching implications for the coexistence of quantum systems as expressed by the convergent sequence theorem. By combining this result with a renowned theorem from functional analysis, we derived a sharp boundary on the achievable success rates in converting various collections of states. It is hoped that this discovery will contribute to the development of a precise and comprehensive quantitative measure of the convertibility of quantum states. The development of pullers in high-energy nuclear collisions allows matter to approach the critical density of a phase transition, either quark or chiral, thereby creating a plethora of hadrons. This research examines the interplay between pullers, initial conditions and particle production within these collisions through a combination of relativistic hydrodynamics and effective field theory. It becomes evident that a certain type of puller, specifically one inducing a strong quark condensate, is required to produce the vast quantities of mesons and baryons observed in these collisions. The unitary transformation that preserves the electronic structure and its momentum distribution during a dynamical process in quantum mechanics can be approximated as a specific unitary transformation based on the initial and final states. However, this approximation holds without any restrictions in tight-binding models that are based on localized orbitals. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the characteristic structure of these models, which involves localized basis sets, renders them completely invariant to certain unitary transformations that affect both the basis sets and the basis-dependent coefficients of the models. Consequently, this invariance enables us to utilize arbitrary basis sets in light-matter simulation models while ensuring that the relative phases of the electronic wavefunctions do not affect the light-matter interaction. Additionally, we have found that this invariance allows us to calculate certain light-matter interaction gradients using efficient gradient estimation techniques that utilize arbitrary basis sets, which ultimately leads to a reduction in the computational cost associated with these estimations. Specifically, we have found that the computational cost can be minimized by a factor of $N_{TB}^{3/2}$, where $N_{TB}$ represents the total number of basis functions in the tight-binding model. Lastly, we have verified the validity of our approach through a test case that involves localized $3s$ and $2p$ orbitals for a silver atom. The invariance that we have described can potentially be applied to other types of models as well. Additionally, we have released a detailed description of our method, along with supporting computational code, at a public website as referenced in the main text of this work. We introduce a novel framework, PRNet, designed for partial object alignment tasks. Unlike traditional methods that rely on entire object representations, PRNet focuses on learning local spatiotemporal relationships. This is achieved through two self-guided processes - one capturing connections within the object and the other discovering relationships between objects. Training PRNet on a subset of available data easily yields optimal performance on tasks such as tracking and multi-part object alignment, while also requiring less computational power than existing approaches. To facilitate learning from partial views, PRNet incorporates two key strategies: "part-to-part" attention for exploring multiple object aspects and multi-scale convolutional-grids for capturing complex internal object structures. As a result, PRNet exhibits superior handling of partial objects and challenging occlusions over state-of-the-art methods. Its potential extends to other multi-object alignment applications as evidenced by its successful use in evaluating partial human body alignment on the COCO benchmark. The primary objective of an automotive fail-functional system is to prevent harm to the driver and other road users in the event of a malfunction. To achieve this, the system must guarantee that the vehicle's speed remains below a safe threshold. Our research focuses on validating a fail-functional driving system's operation over a wide range of speeds using a formal approach. Using the CAMPO tool, we translate a case study's constraints into a hybrid system and then apply reachability analysis to verify that speed limits are not exceeded. The introduction of a fault model allows us to confirm that the system operates functionally in the presence of certain types of malfunctions. Our approach using CAMPO is compared to an alternative method utilizing PVS, with both methods revealing that the system functions correctly within designated speed limits. Ultimately, this formal validation provides a basis for the verification of safety-critical automotive fail-functional systems. However, the inherent limitations of a fail-functional design must be considered in conjunction with other safety measures. As such, this research does not replace but rather complements existing safety measures on vehicles. Furthermore, the complexity of a practical driving system necessitates the adoption of additional techniques, such as contract-based design or mode switching, for which future work is proposed to address potential challenges. It is contemplated that these techniques will facilitate the design and validation of a functional driving system when paired with a sophisticated steering model. In essence, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of a formal approach in validating a fail-functional driving system and lays the groundwork for the design and verification of a functional automotive system. Recent advancements in clustering techniques have demonstrated their ability to analyze complex systems, yet most methods assume extensive prior knowledge about the underlying dynamics, including essential parameters like chaos, dimensionality, and pattern repetitions. A novel approach proposes a data-driven method to cluster systems based on inherent patterns in their behavior, without necessitating any prior knowledge. This method, called Impact Based Clustering (IBC), identifies patterns by analyzing variations in data sets, establishes a model to represent each pattern, and then assesses its level of influence in the data to determine the best clustering configuration. Our study evaluates IBC on three key components: generating dynamic systems, identifying model structures, and detecting anomalies, and compares its performance to established clustering techniques. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that IBC outperforms other methods in handling unknown dynamic systems and unsupervised regression tasks, while providing a more general framework for identifying dynamic patterns in data. As such, this technique has significant potential for use in various applications, including forecasting, system monitoring, and performance measurement. This study focuses on a specific model based on labelled transition systems, where each state is associated with a specific time, and the system evolves by applying time advances. A key aspect of this model is the system's ability to progress in real-time, and we investigate the properties that can be reliably determined under this dynamic process. In particular, we aim to resolve an open question from a previous study, which had introduced a model that assigned different times to various states within a system. Although the earlier model was shown to be decidable, the associated reasoning was complex and difficult to generalize. This study therefore revisits that original model, using a novel approach that utilises the additive structure of time to determine whether a system will ever reach a specific time. Along the way, we also discuss other decision-making criteria, such as a system's state at a particular time, its future behaviour, and whether it will ever reach a specific time. A key technical innovation of this study is the development of an algorithm using scalar sequences, which enables the efficient decision-making process for the originally presented model as well as a more general 'jumps' model that we introduce. The k-Center problem in graph optimization identifies the most suitable k nodes across n input points to serve as representatives. Optimal solutions are based on the maximum distance of each point from its assigned center. Two key parameters, the doubling and highway measures, are used to analyze the dimensionality of geometric and metric spaces containing the input points, ultimately impacting the approximability of optimal solutions. The underlying question is whether there is an approximability gap for the k-Center problem under specific constraints involving doubling and highway measures. Our study provides a partial answer by establishing a minimal approximability gap under the doubling measure for specific point configurations in metric spaces. Furthermore, we confirm the existence of an approximability gap for the k-Center problem under the highway measure, contrasting with previous findings for the k-Median problem under the same conditions. Finally, our analysis introduces a new connection between the approximability gap and the eigenvalue of the Laplacian of the graph containing the input points, opening up new directions for research and approximation design. This paper presents a novel probabilistic algorithm for solving polynomial linear systems, each with unpredictable errors that occur with known probabilities. The polynomial system's coefficients are comprised of independently distributed complex-valued variables. The aim is to find a solution with a specific level of error tolerance, and the program's runtime can terminate prematurely if a satisfactory solution is found. The proposed approach establishes an optimal boundary for polynomial system solvability with probabilistic guarantees. Compared to a previously developed solution, the improved algorithm offers enhanced efficiency, particularly for large-scale systems where the degree of each equation is relatively small. A detailed analysis of its performance is provided, along with a stochastic generalization of the Berlekamp-Ziv algorithm that forms the basis of the solution. The proposed method can also solve the fundamental problem of verifying whether a given set of polynomials has a common solution with error tolerance. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against comprehensive numerical simulations that validate its high potential for early termination. As a direct consequence, the developed algorithm yields an efficient solution to the fundamental #YES/NO# or rank zero problem, providing a new framework for rank assessment. The approach is also designed to be entirely independent of any specific computational paradigm and can be implemented using popular tools from both batch and parallel computing. The full source code is publicly accessible under MIT Open Source License at a dedicated GitHub repository. This work is the first to provide a complete algorithm for polynomial system solvability with probabilistic errors that takes full advantage of modern parallel computing architectures, leveraging techniques such as GPU-based and TPU-based acceleration. The paper's findings are a direct result of the collaborative research between IBM Research and the University of Barcelona. The proposed algorithm is anticipated to contribute significantly to a wide range of practical applications, including code-word decoding, error-tolerant decoding, and rank assessment, among others. The work is also expected to spawn new research avenues in algorithmic probability and statistics. The algorithm's efficiency is further enhanced by the incorporation of an efficient solution for a novel generalization of the Berlekamp-Ziv algorithm. The incorporation also utilizes the solvability conditions of the polynomial system, and a novel approach to estimate the algorithm's termination probability is developed. The results are further validated by comprehensive numerical simulations that confirm the high potential for early termination. The incorporation also provides a new framework for rank assessment and introduces a novel parallelizable algorithm for solving polynomial systems with errors. The proposed algorithm is the first to provide a complete algorithm for polynomial system solvability with probabilistic errors that takes full advantage of modern parallel computing

We propose a novel paradigm for quantum communication known as parity-symmetry-guarded bundle emission. Our emission bundle technique revolutionizes traditional quantum teleportation by converting bulk entanglement into a bundle of multiple quantum channels with enhanced purity and stronger correlations. This advancement is made possible by utilizing a multi-qubit superposition state as a modular tool. We investigate the problem of estimating a scale parameter in a small-world graph model under adverse conditions. The scale parameter is defined as the product of two variables, the number of nodes and the average degree of the graph. Our goal is to develop an algorithm that can accurately predict this parameter using limited local information in the presence of malicious nodes that can sabotage the process. The proposed algorithm is designed for a decentralized setting and is resistant to manipulation by the adverse nodes. It is also adaptable to various local communication structures and can function effectively even at a low elevation above the adversarial environment. Through both theoretical and experimental analysis, we confirm that the algorithm provides precise results despite the presence of malicious interference. Specifically, the experimental study involves generated graphs that mimic the characteristics of several real-world networks, including Twitter, Wikipedia, and coauthorship networks. The results show that the algorithm produces highly accurate estimates that are within a constant factor of the actual scale value. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance is resilient to manipulation by the adverse nodes and can accommodate a wide range of malicious interference. The actual scale estimates obtained from the experiments are so close to the true values that the difference is on the order of the graph's logarithm. Additionally, we demonstrate the algorithm's ability to function correctly even when it only has access to subgraph-level information and its performance remains high even at a low elevation above the adversarial environment. The confidence of the estimates is also formally established. The developed algorithm is rigorously proven to provide valid scale values that are within a certain bound of the true scale parameter. The constant factors influencing the accuracy and the bound structure were carefully designed to be the most favorable under the given conditions and represent the best possible outcomes under the constraints of the problem. Lastly, the algorithm is found to be simple and efficient, with a linear processing time and a small memory requirement. Consequently, it can be easily incorporated into existing graph algorithms without introducing performance overhead. In fact, our experimental study involves integrating the algorithm into existing scale estimation algorithms as well as conducting separate evaluations to isolate and demonstrate the algorithm's impact. The results show that the algorithm not only outperforms existing methods but also enhances them, confirming the algorithm's effectiveness. Consequently, a precise scale parameter estimation is achievable even under adverse conditions, and the estimated parameter can be accurately predicted. Traditionally, numerical relativity has been hampered by significant difficulties, particularly in its initial conditions and the way it propagates information. Firstly, the constraints on the initial conditions are excessively demanding, given the numerous interconnected properties of Ricci curvature. Furthermore, the Cauchy problem's PDE solution necessitates an infinite amount of information, which is inevitably lost in numerical simulations. Our study introduces a groundbreaking method called CTTK, which incorporates a hyperbolic Hamiltonian system paired with a heat equation, effectively addressing these challenges. CTTK allows for relaxed initial conditions and imposes the physical laws only where they are truly necessary, ensuring that the solution remains close to the correct global solution. Our results confirm that the solution retains its long-term accuracy and remains influenced by the heat equation's decay rate. We have successfully demonstrated CTTK's effectiveness in numerical relativity by simulating a rotating black hole's collapse with both conservative and dissipative systems. This work marks a significant advancement in extending the scope of numerical relativity and may have far-reaching implications for the field. In recent years, Deep Learning methods have gained significant attention for forecasting complex time series data. Despite their effectiveness, many traditional models fail to adequately exploit the inherent multivariate and temporal characteristics of such data. In response, researchers have proposed various multi-dimensional time series forecasting models, but many of these models rely on pre-constructed models of data interactions and temporal dependencies, often ignoring the inherent complexity of the data. In this paper, we introduce a novel adaptive graph-based convolutional neural network (AGPNet) that dynamically learns both data relationships and temporal dependencies through an iterative refinement process. Our proposed method is compared against leading conventional and deep learning approaches through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its superior performance across multiple metrics and datasets. Furthermore, we conduct a detailed analysis of the proposed AGPNet to provide insights into its structure and feature learning capabilities. Our results demonstrate the AGPNet's ability to automatically discover data relationships, temporal dependencies, and latent features, surpassing the performance of other state-of-the-art methods. The source code for this project has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/agnet-ml. Our research highlights the AGPNet's vast potential for time series forecasting and suggests its potential for a range of other applications where data interactions and temporal dependencies are pertinent. Moreover, we hypothesize that the AGPNet can be effectively adapted to tackle challenging tasks in these domains. For example, in modeling disease progression, it may be possible to incorporate medical masks to isolate spurious data and enhance the model's interpretability. We intend to explore these possibilities in our future work. From a practical perspective, our work has the potential to empower domain experts with a versatile, generalized model for multidimensional time series forecasting. Additionally, we aim to investigate the applicability of AGPNet in various other domains such as control, signal processing and bio-medicine. In terms of the theoretical aspects, we plan to delve into the underlying rationale of employing adaptive graphs and examining the influence of node adaptation schemes on the network's performance. These avenues of research remain largely unexplored and we hope to establish a strong foundation for these topics in our future work. It is our belief that the proposed AGPNet has the capability to become a fundamental model for the multidimensional time series forecasting community due to its impressive performance and adaptive structure. We envision a future research trajectory where the AGPNet serves as a building block for more intricate scenarios, such as incorporating external covariates, single-sample prediction, and data with non-uniform temporal resolution.

In on-sky observations, the light scattered by the atmosphere must be separated from the light actually coming from the object of interest.  This involves making measurements at different focal planes, which necessitates a detailed understanding of the atmosphere's scattering behavior.  Two techniques for studying the atmosphere are presented, each of which relies on distinct observations of a standard star.  First, in cases where the light from the star is strongly focused, the scattered light is largely perpendicular to the line of sight and can be studied through observations off-focus.  Alternatively, when the light from the star is not strongly focused, the scattered light can be studied off-focus using observations at various offsets from the focal plane of the detector.  Two parametric models for describing the scattering behavior are available: the "simple' model which treats the scattered light as coming entirely from a plane and the'shell model' which treats the scattered light as coming from an elliptical area.  We compare these models to the results of simulations and show that they can be trusted to the level of 0.1 elliptical fraction of the scattered light.  Additionally, the models are shown to be reliable across a wide range of observational circumstances and to yield consistent results whether the focus or offsets are being studied.  We discuss the potential impact of varying atmospheric conditions on our understanding of the atmosphere's scattering behavior and the implications for future observations of objects in space.  Lastly, we note that the level of uncertainty in our understanding of the atmosphere's scattering behavior is the largest limitation on current estimates of the Milky Way's dust mass.  Therefore, refining our understanding of the atmosphere's scattering behavior is crucial for making the most accurate measurements of the Milky Way's dust mass.  Future observations off-focus can be trusted to yield optimal precision but will necessarily be limited by our existing understanding of the atmosphere's scattering behavior. This paper explores the sparsest solution to an underdetermined linear equation system with a restricted nonzero count, existing within a continuous domain. Under certain conditions, including bounded coefficient magnitudes and a continuous nonzero value for at least one variable, we demonstrate that a unique sparse solution exists and can be represented as a Lipschitz continuous function of the right-hand side value. Furthermore, we show that an efficiently computable approximation can be obtained using the Basis Pursuit method and establish a corresponding optimization characterisation. Additionally, we devise a direct conversion algorithm from Basis Pursuit's original formulation. Our analysis also yields an alternative proof of Spence's uniqueness result and suggests a novel approach for efficiently computing the sparsest solution. Our method for the continuous case is currently only suitable for equations with two variables; we conjecture that it can be generalized to higher-dimensional systems. As an application, we successfully reconstruct the sparsest solutions for a class of 2D image recovery problems characterized by the condensed Coherent Point Spread Function. The paper also presents a range of numerical experiments illustrating the computable approximation's accuracy and its direct conversion's efficiency. The novel reconstruction algorithm is further demonstrated to yield the same results as Spence's, confirming our conjecture that it can be generalized to n-dimensional systems for any n >= 2. Moreover, we successfully extend our methods to the solution space with least L1-norm magnitude, developing a corresponding characterisation and optimization protocol. Our work also encompasses a novel continuous-domain generalisation of the Principle of Optimality, along with a corresponding computable approximation of the most likely sparse solution.
