P4 has become the standard language for designing forwarders in software-defined networking environments. A versatile language allows network designers to create customized packet processing systems with programmable forwarding elements. Despite its benefits, designing a P4-based system can be a complex and laborious process, especially when there is a need for significant modifications to the switch architecture. This paper presents a novel open-source framework that streamlines the compilation of P4 programs into reliable, high-performance forwarding components. The proposed compiler, P416, is based on the P4-16 language standard and incorporates a novel approach to automatically converting program match and action tables into efficient hardware implementations. By leveraging SMT solvers, P416 can identify optimal solutions for high-performance match-action tables and provide multiple implementation choices with different resource requirements. Experimental results confirm the efficiency and flexibility of the P416 compiler in performing hardware-like traffic processing and match-action operations. The P416 compiler's open-source code is available at https://github.com/p416-compiler/p416. The experimental results are available at https://github.com/p416-compiler/p416-results. Additional information can be found at https://p416-compiler.w3.ccs.ntu.edu.sg. Extensions of this research are presented in the papers 'P4V: an Adaptive Buffering System for Programmable Forwarders' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.0071), 'P4B: Batch Processing for Efficient Programmable Forwarders' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.0072), and 'P4SW: a Swift Visitor for Efficient Programmable Forwarders' (https://arxiv.org/.abs/2201.0073). The RT0 approximations don't fully utilize the available degrees of freedom when solving the convection-diffusion equation, particularly in cases involving a low diffusion coefficient and structured quadrilateral elements. To address this issue, a direct imposition of the continuity of the convection vector field is introduced into the RT0 approximation space. This modification results in the use of all available degrees of freedom and yields first-order discrete convection vectors, similar to the reference solution. Numerous numerical tests confirm that this approach provides more accurate solutions than standard RT0 approximations, especially in singular-perturbation cases. Furthermore, the implemented scheme is blind to the diffusion coefficient and only relies on being below a certain threshold relative to the convection coefficient. This scheme has potential applications in similar problems and can be extended for use with other finite elements. Additionally, a related discussion on discretising the streamlines of an advection-diffusion equation is included. The included code allows users to easily replicate the proposed scheme using the FreeFEM++ language. A theoretical validation of the approach is provided in the associated journal article (arXiv2206.0422). This work can also provide improved results for similar equations such as the Helmholtz decomposition and the Maxwell's equations. Lastly, the provided C code can be used to give more accurate approximations of the vector convection field for the convection-diffusion equation in structured quadrilateral elements. A recently introduced method called Continuous-Phase Runge-Kutta (CPRK) has been shown to be a highly efficient approach for solving certain continuous-time state-space models that experience random disturbances. Building on the successful application of the CPRK algorithm, this study develops new optimization techniques for similar dynamic models that contain uncertainties. These techniques draw their name from a fundamental concept in numerical analysis, where the smooth evolution of a function over time is referred to as its 'continuity'. One of the proposed algorithms is a direct extension of the CPRK method, while the other two methods, known as CITE and CITE-G, are more akin to the successive minimalization algorithm (SUMO) and the successive minimalization algorithm with guarantees (SUMG) respectively. These algorithms successfully address the existing limitations of the CPRK method by taking the model's smooth evolution into account when optimizing a performance metric, a criterion that was previously known to be multi-modal in state-space models experiencing random disturbances. As a result, the proposed algorithms offer improved performance and faster computational speed than existing methods such as the successive minimalization algorithm (SUM) and the successive minimalization algorithm with guarantees (SUMG). Furthermore, the researchers have developed theoretical arguments to demonstrate the reliability of the proposed algorithms, proving that their local optimality guarantees are robust to minor variations in the model and show that these guarantees are more precise when the model is more accurate. Building on these results, the researchers have also developed new convergence bounds for the algorithms, proving that their convergence speed is directly proportional to the number of iterations performed. Finally, the study verifies the efficacy of the proposed algorithms through numerical simulations of a real-world application, specifically an electronic tag used in bovine identification. When tested against existing methods, the researchers found that CITE and CITE-G outperformed them in every respect, delivering better performance, faster processing, and more accurate results than existing methods. Notably, the researchers found that both CITE and CITE-G performed equally well, suggesting that they are interchangeable. The study expects that these algorithms will be widely adopted in the simulation and testing of advanced driver-assistance systems and the design of intelligent transportation systems, where more accurate state estimation is critical for safe and efficient travel. Conversely, when the constant force is decreased from a non-zero value, the size of the Wada basins shrinks and then disappears at a critical point, where it begins to grow again in an opposite manner. What's more, this research found that extremely weak friction can not only alter the shape of the Wada basins but also increase their connected areas and even create new channels within them. The study provides new insights into the characteristics of Wada basins in a three-dimensional chaotic scattering system. If the VLB mass exceeds a specific threshold, its taste-alignment becomes resistant to decay in vacuum, and its interaction with other particles in a taste-dependent manner, resulting in potentially detectable signatures in particle colliders and astronomical environments. A vital component of IoT infrastructure, Network Function Virtualization, ensures the smooth functioning of services and systems by protecting against malicious attacks, particularly DDoF which wreaks havoc on IoT devices, necessitating robust protection mechanisms to prevent further destruction. To counter DDoF, a novel attack detection system called NBcoded has been devised, utilizing Graph Attention Networks and combining it with Naive Bayes classifier in an encoder-decoder framework. By generating feature maps from attack signatures and mapping them to discrete codes via a special decoder, NBcoded effectively detects and differentiates various attack types, encompassing DoS, Scan, Uplike, and Bi-Directional Traffic attacks. With its ability to adapt to resource constraints of small devices, NBcoded is characterized by its compact size and generalizability, as evidenced by the extensive experiments conducted on 14 IoT datasets. Additionally, the proportion of false positives and negatives is remarkably low, at 0.002% and 0.001% respectively. This superior performance means NBcoded can effectively protect IoT applications from harmful DDoF attacks, making it an excellent choice for implementing a real-world IoT security system. This study presents an analytical method for extracting biologic movement within video footage. Consequently, the researchers concluded that thorough understanding of the scene and its elements is necessary for accurate movement detection. This study by the ATLAS collaboration employed the full dataset of $pp$ collisions collected during Run 2 (5.36 inverse femtobarns at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV) to search for heavy, long-lived, charged particles that interact strongly with other fundamental particles. The particles in question could be as large as 900 GeV and have lifespans ranging from zero to 15 cm, with charges of 1.9 to 2.4 and are modeled using the symbols $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{L}$, respectively. The search involves two complementary methods analyzing the properties of tracks and their combinations in events containing at least one high-energy electron or photon output. No individual anomalies were detected and statistical significance greater than 3 standard deviations was achieved across a vast range of the $\mathcal{E}$-$\mathcal{L}$ plane, with some areas under scrutiny reaching as high as 3.8 standard deviations. A wide range of models based on first-generation particles, including a hypothetical particle similar to a gluon but with a long lifespan and an alternative model featuring a dark Higgs boson that breaks symmetry in dark matter, were specifically examined to generate predicted results for this study. Well-established techniques in evolutionary optimization, such as multi-objective optimization and problem bi-objectivization, have been refined over time but still rely on overly simplistic assumptions regarding the optimal solution phenotypes. Specifically, these methods assume the existence of disjoint regions, each containing a single optimal solution, yet this approach fails to account for more complex phenotypes observed in real-world tasks. This study investigates the variability of phenotypic behavior in solving multi-solution optimization tasks, revealing that (1) phenotypic variation is a common phenomenon in solving optimization problems; (2) phenotypic variation has a positive correlation with the number of optimal solutions and the dimensionality of the search space; (3) population size has a positive effect on the diversity of phenotypes; (4) different optimization problems exhibit distinct phenotypic patterns due to the inherent nature of the objectives and interaction between the objectives and genotypes; and (5) phenotypic variation can be harnessed using techniques such as phenotypic ga, which can lead to improved convergence speed and quality of results. Our results indicate the necessity for more comprehensive theories underpinning optimization with multi-solution phenotypes and suggest further research is required to explore the potential of phenotypic variation in tackling real-world tasks. Based on these findings, we also propose several open research problems. Finally, the code and data used for this study are publicly available for reproduction of the results. The contribution of this work is threefold: (i) it examines the phenotypic behavior in multi-solution optimization; (ii) it highlights the limitations and unrealistic assumptions of current optimization methods; (iii) it paves the way for future research on more realistic and complex phenotypic behavior in optimization tasks. The research is expected to the benefit the field of optimization. The use of Large Binary Optics on the second generation ground-based telescopes is crucial for minimizing speckle-related issues and achieving high resolution. Although conventional techniques for reducing speckle noise have limitations, a novel method known as the Rapid Atmospheric Self-coherent Camera (RASCAM) has been developed to effectively utilize Large Binary Optics. Recent experiments using this system on the Santa Cruz extreme adaptive optics facility testbed have successfully demonstrated its capability in high velocity focal plane wavefront control of residual speckles through a 32 actuator RASCAM with a 4.64 micron pixel size and a 2.88 x 2.88 field of view. Furthermore, parabolic correlation wavefront sensing was employed to achieve impressive results, with a Strehl ratio of 12.4%, 0.66 Jy/Hz in an 8.5 GHz bandwidth around 2.2 microns, and a high resolution of 0.56 mas after removing speckle noise. Moreover, experiments have revealed the significant impact of speckle noise on transition phase closure and the effectiveness of RASCAM in preserving transition phase closure even under harsh speckle noise conditions. In fact, a 0.62 reduction in loss of transition phase closure has been achieved with RASCAM. These groundbreaking findings mark an important milestone for the future of second generation ground-based telescopes and will significantly contribute to the reduction of speckle noise, allowing for more efficient speckle reduction techniques to be deployed on the path towards the Holy Grail of second generation ground-based telescopes, the Extremely Large Telescope. A substantial body of research is devoted to the concept of calculable systems, a category that encompasses a specific type of dynamical system possessing a calculable structure. This theoretical framework has numerous real-world applications, including artificial intelligence, computational biology, and information systems. Prior studies primarily focused on the computational aspects of calculable systems. In contrast, this paper delves into the fundamental question of how these systems' underlying structures are computed. To this end, we introduce a general approach to defining complex system hierarchies using expandable models and derive a formula for determining the height of these hierarchies. Our methodology is universally applicable to any calculable system and has practical implications for information systems, as demonstrated by a case study centered on Wikipedia's hyperlink structure. By analyzing Wikipedia's hyperlink network, we calculated its hierarchy and found that the site's popularity peaks at a height of approximately nine levels. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm for systematically calculating hierarchies in general expandable models and thoroughly evaluate its performance using real-world datasets. Our findings reveal that this algorithm reaches its performance ceiling at a height of three levels for systems with directly connected nodes and four levels for those with indirect connections. In sum, our work establishes a concrete framework for understanding calculable systems' structural composition and provides a practical approach to analyzing complex system hierarchies. To facilitate further research and applications, we make available a publicly accessible online platform for calculating hierarchies, along with the source code and empirical results. We conduct a thorough examination of the Three-Body Problem's forecasting capabilities, specifically focusing on a statistical model that builds upon existing analytical solutions. To achieve this, we introduce the Flux-driven statistical model, which estimates the probabilities of binary outcomes entrapping a third object based on initial conditions. The accuracy of this model is evaluated through two metrics: the binary escape probability and the binary-escape time distribution. Our analytical findings are refined and compared against numerical simulations from the N-Body Problem. Furthermore, we investigate the binary escape times in the range of $t\approx 10-20$ in semi-major axes $a$ under three initial conditions: escape, temporary capture, and permanent capture. Notably, we observe good agreement between our analytical calculations and numerical simulations from the N-Body Problem, with errors typically less than 10%, except for small escape times with errors not exceeding 20%. Moreover, we find that times with errors less than a 5% threshold include those from the N=10, N=20, and N=30 numerical simulations. To better understand the dynamics of turbulent flows, researchers have developed new theoretical frameworks in recent years, but they often neglect to account for the effects of viscosity. However, since turbulence is inevitably driven by the interaction with the surrounding flow and ultimately affected by the walls of the container holding the flow, it is inevitable that the effects of viscosity will eventually be felt. To address this, the existing theories need to be combined with the Kolmogorov framework in a way that accounts for the effects of viscosity on small-scale turbulent movements. Specifically, this study explores the interactions between turbulent flows and their boundaries, and as a result, develops a new model for understanding the behavior of turbulent flows at all scales. We establish two fundamental criteria for sound probabilistic lambda-typed evaluation frameworks. Firstly, we prove that the desired outcome is uniquely determined by the input program and its associated probabilities. Secondly, we establish that the proposed framework respects the inherent logical meaning underlying the probabilistic lambda-calculus. Our work specifically builds upon two previous studies, namely Wadler's resource types and Abramsky's categorical semantics for the probabilistic lambda-calculus. Utilizing a detailed analysis of the probabilistic lambda-calculus's proof-theoretic properties, we demonstrate that the proposed frameworks adhere to two key criteria: type and proof soundness, and we further show that the categorical semantics is constructed in a way that respects the inherent logical meaning. Consequently, we prove that the two strongest known criteria for probabilistic type systems are both inherently incompatible with each other. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework is the strongest known type system that is consistent with the probabilistic lambda-calculus's proof-theoretic structure while being preserved by its categorical semantics. Lastly, we introduce and study a new type system that combines the hybrid of Wadler's resource types and Maksimovic and Basu's local choice types, yielding a system that is more expressive than each individual framework alone. Utilizing an in-depth proof, we prove that this new combined type system does not violate the two key criteria for sound evaluation frameworks. Moreover, we show that its associated denial and local choice types, in the absence of resource types, preserve the categorical semantics and that these types are an optimal way to define an adequate and strongest possible hybrid system. Lastly, we introduce an efficient type inference algorithm for the combined system and demonstrate its correctness through a series of rigorous proofs. Specifically, we definitively establish the fundamental relationship between the bounds of a program's denotational and operational probabilistic meanings. Our work specifically provides a novel inference algorithm for hybrid local choice and denial types with the guarantee that the resulting types are at most a factor of $O(\log p)$ wider than what is necessary for sound evaluation, where $p$ is the program's associated probability bound. This performance guarantee significantly improves upon the existing known bound of $O(\sqrt{p})$. Ultimately, we believe that our study will provide valuable insights into the design of an efficient type inference algorithm for probabilistic programs in higher-order programming languages. This study focuses on the area of imitation learning, specifically tackling tasks where an agent is unable to receive instructions because the instructions would require an understanding of the expert's perspective, expertise that can't be obtained. We present a novel approach, 'MIMO,' where an agent learns to mimic various behaviors by observing multiple experts working on distinct tasks. Unlike traditional expert demonstration methods, MIMO doesn't involve the expert's actions but instead relies on the observations from each expert. We test this approach with three practical scenarios: 1) crossing roads for self-driving vehicles, 2) cooking tasks in a kitchen, and 3) navigating through forest paths. MIMO successfully applies to these tasks and others without needing task-specific algorithms, expert-specific modeling, or reinforcement learning. MIMO's performance is comparable to state-of-the-art performance in these scenarios, indicating its efficiency and effectiveness. We also investigate MIMO's capacity to generalize between tasks and note that its success is largely driven by the expert behaviors being consistent within each task. We hope MIMO can serve as a basic framework for addressing imitation learning challenges that require an outsider's perspective. The code for this project is publicly available at https://github.com/yilundong/mimo.assistant

Furthermore, the results from previous studies on privacy breaches in minimum and maximum values are expanded and improved, providing more accurate estimates through the utilization of a novel dependence metric.  Additionally, the total privacy expenditure under sequential composition is determined, offering a significant improvement over existing bounds in the literature.  Lastly, the effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a real-world application involving a dependent characteristic privacy breach of a database containing geographical data.  The method enables the creation of an accurate privacy metric that is more refined and targeted, addressing a notable shortcoming in previous research that had only considered independent characteristic privacy.  Consequently, this approach facilitates more precise and practical evaluations of privacy breaches in real-world settings.  The approach, however, does not preclude the possibility of underestimating privacy breaches and thus remains conservative.  As such, this framework is anticipated to contribute positively to the study of dependent characteristic privacy and one-sided differential privacy. This note provides a clearer definition of robust shift equivalence in row-finite directed graphs and C*-algebras, alongside key reminders of its underlying principles. It also demonstrates that trivializing infinite path products over specific orbits in Z can be expressed through a particular type of shift equivalence, especially when dealing with graphs featuring only two vertices. Additionally, we highlight an ongoing open question concerning whether shift equivalence is equivalent to topological conjugacy in this specific context. It is also noted that proving this conjecture would have significant consequences, including the establishment of new examples of non-trivially shift equivalent C*-algebras, as well as the creation of topologically equivalent but non-weakly equivalent compact abelian groups. Furthermore, we propose a broader definition of shift equivalence that encompasses any group, as well as its potential implications on reduced crossed products of C*-algebras. This investigation is motivated by a broader hypothesis that shift equivalence is simply topological conjugacy across all groups. If proven true, this hypothesis would yield numerous exceptional cases in group theory. Lastly, we suggest a number of questions and potential research directions that this problem poses. We are dealing with a issue of sequential data where the order of data is crucial for accurate analysis and this order is not present in STIP. The results showed that long short-term memory outperformed long-term memory, fast text classifier, random forest, support vector machine, and vector machine. We discovered that adding progressive reinforcement labels enhanced the accuracy by 10% or more compared to using human labels alone. We also used the output as additional information to assist classification on unlabeled data and achieved higher accuracy than models that did not employ this approach. The study demonstrated the effectiveness of long short-term memory in acquiring sequential temporal knowledge and its potential to be utilized in various other tasks. Achieving an optimal balance between economic and economic well-being is essential during an epidemic. We show that countermeasures implemented at the onset of the outbreak and maintained until the number of cases levels off naturally minimize both the extent of the epidemic and the cumulative cost of countermeasures, and this applies across all types of outbreaks. The desired countermeasure duration is calculated for outbreaks characterized by a linear, random and nonlinear progression of cases, and its feasibility is assessed through various countermeasures including culling, social distancing and medication. Furthermore, we illustrate the significance of implementing countermeasures in the context of an epidemic mimicking a complex network and a particular type of nonlinear outbreak. The effectiveness of our approach is also examined in the context of an outbreak that has not yet peaked. Additionally, we provide a corollary that can be useful in analyzing other types of catastrophic events such as wildfires, invasive species and invasive plants. From a practical perspective, we outline specific countermeasures that can be utilized to mitigate the spread of COVID-19, measles and influenza. The method introduced here can detect the critical countermeasure duration for a wide range of outcomes and can serve as a practical tool for policymakers. The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) depends on vast amounts of data, making dataset quality a critical factor in ML model performance. Nonetheless, assessing an ML dataset's quality is a complex task due to its vastness and variability. Once an issue arises with the dataset, it spreads to the training process, compromising the ML model's capabilities. Consequently, the problem is more profound than simply addressing data quality or model reliability issues in isolation; rather, it requires a comprehensive approach that takes both aspects into consideration. Given this multifaceted challenge, a unified framework for diagnosing dataset issues is needed. In this context, we introduce a new metric, the Shapley significance score (SSS), for evaluating dataset effectiveness by analyzing how a dataset's quality impacts ML model performance on an task-by-task basis. Utilizing the SSS metric, we can identify crucial data samples that contribute to the ML model's performance and isolate issues within the dataset, allowing for a data-quality improvement process that is informed by ML model behavior. Through experiments, the SSS metric has been shown to outperform existing dataset validation methods, empowering ML developers to make informed decisions about dataset quality and model design. Furthermore, this approach streamlines the dataset-quality and ML design optimization process, thus accelerating model deployment. In addition, the proposed framework fosters a more collaborative environment in ML development by incorporating data quality and model effectiveness into a shared objective function. In particular, our framework facilitates collaborative optimization between the data quality and model design stages, thus enabling joint training and a shared objective. It is observed that tuning dataset quality and model design simultaneously yields the best results. Recent research has focused on enumerative geometry, uncovering novel algebraic relationships between statistical models, random processes, and discrete structures like partitions, trees, and posets. This new area of study is closely related to topological combinatorics, examining the underlying statistical model's topology. As a case in point, enumerative geometry revealed a topological structure for the collection of all tree-valued arrays, yielding a critical topological distinction between marginal Poisson law and gamma law. Similarly, the topology of poset-valued arrays led to an enumeration-based proof that the Gaussian law is uniquely distinct from other discrete laws. Furthermore, enumerative geometry made connections between the topological structure of interaction forests and free groups. These findings suggest that enumerative geometry can uncover fundamental, topology-driven characteristics of statistical models, thereby identifying key features that models should exhibit and failing to classify models solely based on symmetry. This approach can be extended to other models, such as copula models, as demonstrated by an examination of models for simultaneous rank data. The material presented is an introduction to a current research project, aiming to establish a general framework for the topology of model classes. This project involves collaborative work with A. Buc Calderon, M. Dukes, M. S. Shah, and R. Yilmaz. The proposed framework will be used to derive new enumerative geometry methods for analyzing model goodness-of-fit and quasi-order. This research focuses on examining how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn.  Initial findings reveal that at low pressures (up to 2 GPa), Mn$_3$Sn maintains its characteristic of having no net magnetization while exhibiting a finite anomalous Hall effect.  Utilizing neutron spectroscopy, the system's magnetic structure was identified as having two magnetostructurally equivalent states below 80 K, which is in contrast to a single state observed in Mn$_3}Sn at high pressure.  Additionally, the observed anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn under pressure can be attributed to its chiral magnetic helicity, which supports the concept that pressure has the potential to regulate the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn by inducing a structurally related but magnetostructurally distinct state.  Moreover, our analysis demonstrates that the pressure-driven collapse of the normal Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn is analogous to that observed in Mn$_3$Ge and is a typical phenomenon in this type of material.  Lastly, the goal of achieving zero net magnetization while completely eliminating the anomalous Hall effect in these types of materials has been identified as a viable pursuit, supported by the discovery in Mn$_3$Sn at high pressure where both properties are not present. Relation extraction is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a crucial step in forming comprehensive knowledge databases. A relation extraction system can be viewed as a function that identifies the connection between two entities within a specific text. Research has shown that neural network-based methods outperform traditional approaches and even expert annotations, and have achieved remarkable results in large-scale machine learning tasks. However, numerous challenges remain unsolved, such as limited training data, domain shifts, and the complexity of relationships. To address these issues, advancements in neural network design have made significant progress. Despite significant research, there is a lack of a comprehensive and systematic understanding of neural network-based relation extraction systems. This thesis provides an in-depth summary of Neural Network-Based Relation Extraction systems and contributes to the state-of-the-art in the field by presenting a comparative analysis of different designs. Through experiments on typical benchmarks, the effectiveness of various models is demonstrated, ultimately shedding light on the underlying principles and offering insights into future developments in the field. Ultimately, this thesis showcases the capability of neural network-based relation extraction systems in achieving exceptional performance on benchmark datasets, such as Bernie and TechData. The findings of this study may be useful to the relation extraction community and have potential applications in related areas, such as text summarization and question answering. Additionally, the findings may be employed in other challenging natural language processing tasks characterized by limited training data. Lastly, the relation extraction system developed as part of this research may be utilized for knowledge acquisition and subsequent integration into extensive knowledge databases, such as DBpedia and Wikidata. This study examines a mixed Steklov-Robin problem for the Laplace operator in a partially accessible domain with a boundary divided into three distinct sections: an accessible area, an impermeable area with a given boundary function, and several small or tiny orifices where the accessible area meets the impermeable area. 

A characterisation is developed for the first non-trivial eigenvalue of this problem, taking into account various scenarios involving the accessibility of these orifices, whether they are small or tiny, and the associated boundary conditions. 

Additionally, two new eigenvalue problems are formulated in the context of an impermeable sphere with a partially accessible surface and a partially porous body with an impermeable boundary. 

Key findings are also presented about how these eigenvalues change in response to external influences, including the size and placement of orifices, and theoretical solutions are formulated for these problems. 

Several numerical experiments are conducted to verify the proposed theories and observe the effects of orifice dimensions on eigenvalue behavior. 
Finally, intriguing comparisons are made between the proposed theorems and existing ones for an entirely accessible domain, and the implications of these results for quantum mechanics and seismic imaging are discussed. 

In particular, our research suggests that reflecting on established theories and practices can yield novel insights and suggestions for future research. 

Significantly, our study reveals the importance of focusing on the physical structure of a problem and the underlying mathematical framework to uncover new perspectives and approaches. 

The main contributions of this research are the proposed theorems, which offer a comprehensive understanding of the proposed model, and a publicly accessible code for computing eigenvalues and brightness factors. 
The research has been collaboratively published in arXiv:2202.06738 and arXiv:2201.11552.

Our annotations differ from standard diagnosis tasks by also capturing background information, allowing for a deeper understanding of the relationships between chest structures and background content. This research explores the relationships between Euler characteristics, the Thurston norm, and hyperbolic volume for a specific type of tight contact manifolds, which are also reflected in the corresponding cohomology of tight contact frameworks. Specifically, we investigate tight contact structures on certain classes of 3-manifolds derived from orientable surface link complements and show that their interactions are governed by a set of consistent patterns. Additionally, we derive a direct relationship between the Euler characteristics of tight contact frameworks and the hyperbolic volumes of their underlying manifolds. Furthermore, we establish a correlation between the coefficients of the Euler characteristics and the weights of the Thurston norms, which are influenced by the genus of the bounding surface. This study provides a thorough characterization of the Euler characteristics and the hyperbolic volumes of tight contact frameworks, thereby accomplishing two key objectives. Initially, we establish a complete classification of the Euler characteristics for specific tight contact frameworks on surface link complements by employing a novel extension of the classical Dehn surgery formula. Secondly, we devise a method to calculate the hyperbolic volume of a tight contact structure on any surface link complement through an extension of an earlier idea proposed by Mrowka and House, which incorporates connections between the Euler characteristics of tight contact frameworks and the hyperbolic volumes of their underlying manifolds. As a result, the findings of this research provide a comprehensive geometric interpretation of the coefficients present in the Euler characteristics of tight contact frameworks on surface link complements. Moreover, the conclusions of this work offer a profound insight into the nature of the hyperbolic volume of a tight contact structure on any surface link complement. To successfully navigate a complex environment, a visual navigation system must strike a balance between exploring its surroundings and focusing on information that helps it achieve its goals.  While constraints like targeting objects of interest might be inherent in real-world scenarios, many challenges like visual navigation tasks and robot manipulation lack such limitations.  As a result, they often require extensive (explore-all) or targeted (explore-by-reach) exploration methods which can be inefficient without prior knowledge of the environment's features.  To address this limitation, our approach, called explore-by-learning, employs a reinforcement learning framework that uses a unique objective function to eliminate unnecessary environmental details and concentrate on relevant information for achieving the desired outcomes.  By incorporating a data-theoretic regularizer, this objective function imposes a penalty for collecting redundant data along the way, with the result that the learning system focuses its attention on the most rewarding information for achieving its goals.  As a result, the learnable policy achieves optimal performance with significantly fewer samples of environmental data, and the associated time and computational resources.  Our experiments, involving both 3D navigation and robot manipulation tasks, have verified the efficacy of our approach, as it significantly improves performance with as few as 10% of the required samples, and delivers comparable performance with extensive data collection.  Moreover, it has enabled successful deployment of robot navigation in new, unseen environments, and facilitated successful manipulation of a robot from randomly selected states.  Thus, our method has delivered efficient, goal-oriented exploration of complex environments with minimal prior knowledge of their features.  As such, it has significant potential for practical application in areas like robot navigation and robot manipulation.  Code for this project is available at https://github.com/yashar-y/EBL. It leverages smart meter data and an unsupervised learning method called Real into Model (RIM), capable of capturing regular pattern in data. Additionally, we outline a data-driven procedure for pinpointing irregular occurrences not captured by the RIM model. By applying this approach on actual recorded data from the Austin Energy power distribution network in Texas, we successfully detected multiple electrical events. Our results confirm the existence of various event types corresponding to distinct statistical patterns, encompassing arcing faults, transformer explosions, and high-power consumption events. TextWorldExpress empowers the development of fast, trainable agents for complex text-based challenges by enabling the rapid repetition of game scenarios and the effortless training of models on vast datasets. The success of Deep Learning approaches for 3D point cloud tasks is heavily influenced by the type of point cloud representation employed. Among the possible representations, high-level features derived from graph convolutional networks (GCN) have gained popularity due to their ability to model global properties and representations. However, current implementations of GCN for point clouds lack effectiveness, particularly when they attempt to learn effective global properties by aggregating local features. To address this issue, we introduce E-GCN, an enhanced graph convolutional network that utilizes an attention mechanism that enables each neighbour to contribute differently to the local feature aggregation. The attention mechanism allows the network to focus more on relevant neighbours, thereby maximizing the quality of local feature aggregation. The experimental results demonstrate the superiority of E-GCN over the existing state-of-the-art methods on three challenging benchmark datasets. The accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/Saurav-31/Effective-GCN. The three benchmark datasets employed for evaluation are O3D-Skeleton, PASCAL-VOC-12, and Scene15. The ability of E-GCN to focus on critical neighbours was visually illustrated through the visualization of the learned attention weights, with the corresponding observations noted in the report. Moreover, the enhancement of E-GCN over the existing methods was quantitatively demonstrated by the analysis of the influence of key components, specifically the attention mechanism, with the observed trends consistent across all evaluation datasets. Furthermore, the ability of E-GCN to consistently achieve top-ranked performance was showcased on four different benchmark datasets, thereby establishing its robustness and reliability. The three datasets where E-GCN consistently demonstrated excellence are: Benchmark, Scene15, and PASCAL-VOC-12. The three key reasons behind the consistency of E-GCN performance were: (i) the ability of GCN to effectively model global properties, (ii) the employment of multi-layer perception (MLP) to capture complex non-local properties, and (iii) the attention mechanism that enhances the quality of local feature aggregation. Recent advancements in cloud-based image processing have led to the development of extremely compact Trojan attacks. Unlike conventional methods requiring network manipulation, these "hostless" attacks directly target neural network structures, allowing for seamless deployment on mobile devices. However, existing hostless Trojan attacks have primarily focused on compromising model reliability and require elaborate auxiliary networks, thereby negating the advantage of compactness. To address this issue, we introduce a new hostless Trojan attack that achieves high performance with minimal additional complexity. Building on existing research, we incorporate gradient channel pruning and utilize transfer learning, leveraging pre-trained convolutional layers. Additionally, we propose a novel backpropagation path that efficiently utilizes these layers, accompanied by an innovative activation-dependent loss function that significantly enhances performance. The result is a highly effective Trojan attack with minimal additional complexity, showcasing a 114% performance boost over state-of-the-art methods. Our findings are backed by extensive experiments and a developed open-source hostless Trojan attack framework. It is expected that our research will facilitate the development of more sophisticated hostless Trojan attacks. The code can be found at: https://github.com/jayie1999/SEMHA.

Recent studies analyzing the exoplanet bulk compositions based on transit light curves and stellar absorption lines have yielded intriguing yet incomplete pictures. Theoretical models suggest many factors can influence a planet's radius at a given mass, including its composition, heating history, and the type of internal energy source. The abundance of volatile elements in a planet's building block materials likely affects its final radius. Researchers have created a comprehensive database of terrestrial-type planet compositions from various protoplanetary disk components, which includes both metal- and silicon-rich materials, enabling them to investigate the role of elemental abundance in shaping a planet's bulk composition. An analysis of 20 exoplanet systems has shown that the models can accurately predict a radius that matches the observed value for low-mass planets (< 3 Earth masses) with a good level of precision. The results indicate that a planet's internal structure is influenced significantly by its composition, as the diversity in radius is largely driven by differences in composition for a given mass, rather than heating history. The analysis finds that small-radius planets are predominantly composed of iron-rich material, whereas high-radius planets are composed of silicon-rich material. The transition from iron-rich to silicon-rich models corresponds to a mass increase of around 5-6 Earth masses. The current understanding of planetary internal structures, which assumes a mass proportion of 3:1 iron to silicate rocks, needs to be revised, as this assumption holds for only about half of the examined exoplanet systems. The research highlights the need to expand the sample to more exoplanet systems, particularly those consisting of small-radius and giant planets. Additionally, studying the abundance of volatile elements in a planet's building block materials remains an unresolved question in planetary science, as it hinges on primitive chondritic materials and carbonaceous chondrites, which have not been fully preserved in the Earth's crust. The research finds no correlation between the stellar metallicity and the radius of the examined exoplanet systems, as the models can accurately predict a radius that matches the observed value regardless of the stellar metallicity. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI). Recent research suggests that leveraging raw CSI can lead to more accurate location estimates compared to relying on CSI features. Nevertheless, raw CSI data is cumbersome and suffers from redundancy, making it difficult for the model to focus on crucial information. This problem can be addressed through the use of self-attention mechanisms in deep learning. This paper proposes the attention-enhanced channel state information network (AECSI-N), a meta-learning based approach for wireless localization that utilizes the attention-enhanced CSI data in a more efficient manner. The AECSI-N method was tested and evaluated on a real municipal building dataset, where the results demonstrate a significant improvement in localization accuracy when compared to the state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the attention weights derived from the trained AECSI-N model were utilized to conduct a detailed analysis and visualization of the importance of different CSI data at various locations in the building. Experimentation revealed that the importance of CSI data varied significantly across different locations in the building. Additionally, the parameters of the attention-enhanced CSI data were observed to exhibit noticeable variations at locations under blockage or heavy shadowing. These findings validate the use of the attention-enhanced CSI data in wireless localization and provide valuable insights for reducing the complexity of CSI data while preserving the critical information required for location estimation. The proposed AECSI-N approach exhibits superior performance and sheds new light on the underlying physical characteristics of the CSI data. The code for this research study is publicly available at this GitHub link: https://github.com/wsn-lab/Attention-Enhanced-CSI-data-for-wireless-localization. The dataset used in this research can be accessed via this link: https://github.com/wsn-lab/TNUB-wireless-localization. The dataset comprises the channel impulse response (CIR) for a municipal building with 15 active transmitter nodes at various locations. The corresponding IEEE 802.11 wireless client data were used to derive the channel state information (CSI) which includes the magnitude and angle of the CIR. The data were collected on a tablet and a IEEE 802.11 wireless client while walking through the building at a pace of about 1.5 miles per hour. The location of the transmitter and receiver were recorded in real-time using a GPS device, and the data were synchronized with the CSI data using a script. The dataset can be used for research purposes by following these instructions: https://github.com/wsn-lab/TNUB

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. We have developed a web-based version, ShinyCOPASI, that allows users to access and interact with COPASI models through a web browser, providing a range of visualization options and providing immediate access to COPASI models for sharing and collaborative use. ShinyCOPASI offers a user-friendly interface for viewing model simulations and their outputs, including species trajectories, phase plots, and error messages, as well as enabling users to upload their own models or access a database of published models for educational purposes. These models can be viewed without the need for any local installation, facilitating educational and outreach activities. Additionally, ShinyCOPASI allows users to run simulations remotely, aiding users who encounter issues running COPASI on their local device. Due to its web-based nature, ShinyCOPASI can be accessed at https://shiny.copasi.org and a comprehensive guide to using ShinyCOPASI is available at https://shiny.copasi.org/help.html. Users can submit their own models to be hosted at https://submit.shiny.copasi.org.

Computing uncertainty in machines is a major area of study in AI, with significant implications for advancements in this field. The field of computing uncertainty in machines, also known as machine ambiguity, has received relatively less attention from researchers. This study examines methods of calculating ambiguity in machines, compiles and analyzes standard techniques for evaluating this metric, and explores the connections between ambiguity and other uncertainty measures. The research also investigates the outcomes of a thorough evaluation of these methods and provides a future research direction. Ultimately, this study serves as a reference point for future studies focused on measuring ambiguity in machines. The research outcomes are available at https://kcovalen.github.io/AmbigMeasurements/. Furthermore, when the compact quantum group is a group $G$, the von Neumann algebra is isomorphic to the group von Neumann algebra $\mathcal{M}(G)$. Additionally, we find that the face maps generate a crossed product action of the compact quantum group on its dual quantum group, enabling us to establish a category equivalence between the compact quantum group's tensor product with its dual and the free product of two compact quantum groups. Finally, we identify the characteristics of a compact quantum group whose dual quantum group is a group $G$. To support these outcomes, we develop a new algebraic approach to studying category functions. We introduce and use various notation and tools, drawing from waltz theory, simplicial geometry, and algebraic topology to describe the operations of category functions. We prove a groupoid version of the strictness theorem for category functions, and develop a stable version of the theorem as well. The theorem is a key discovery in the study of category functions. We investigate the application of the generalized minimum residual method in the context of iterative policy improvement for solving large-scale Markov decision processes. By representing an iterative advantage update as a linear system, we apply GMRES to tackle the challenge of extensive MDPs. From a theoretical standpoint, we establish that each iteration of this approach enhances policy quality. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of incomplete GMRES and propose the concept of 'policy residual'. Through experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of inGMRES, particularly when combined with the Q-decomposition technique, for treating noisy problems and achieving high-performance solutions to MDPs at a batch policy iteration. Scientific studies frequently utilize computer-based modeling to predict complex systems, but accurately comparing these models to real-world data is a difficult task. This difficulty arises from several challenges: firstly, there is often a substantial disparity between the simulated and actual data due to varying resolution levels, secondly, real-world measurements are subject to noise and uncertainty, and thirdly, the evaluation criteria for models are frequently intricate and multi-faceted.

Our proposed method tackles this challenge by allowing for the comparison of computer-based models with respect to real-world data through a detailed analysis of their time-series projections. The theoretical underpinnings of this approach are rooted in its ability to simultaneously handle the aforementioned issues of scale, uncertainty, and complex evaluation criteria. The underlying theory involves an extension of an established concept, known as the Multiple Contour Assessment, which originally addressed two-dimensional data but has now been evolved to accommodate a more comprehensive framework for dealing with three-dimensional data. This framework incorporates time as a pivotal variable in the analysis.

The results demonstrate that this framework is versatile and can seamlessly integrate various validation metrics, noise levels, and real-world data into the model comparison process. Furthermore, it enables the creation of a comprehensive score that reflects the alignment between the simulated data and actual observations across multiple sites. The framework's resilience to noisy data and its ability to effectively compare models under uncertainty have been thoroughly tested and validated through a series of simulations. An open-source software implementation is made available for this purpose. An example illustrating the use of this method in the context of air quality modeling is provided to showcase its practical applications. The framework's potential future developments include integrating external validation, model ensemble techniques, and the incorporation of model parameter uncertainty to further enhance its utility and future research directions. The development of this method is anticipated to have a broad range of applications extending beyond air quality modeling and will likely resonate with numerous other communities engaged in computer-based modeling. The theoretical underpinnings of this approach have the potential to be extended and applied to various other fields, such as climate modeling, epidemiology, and neuroscience. The general strategy of utilizing multiple features for model evaluation is a universally applicable strategy that can be transferred to various contexts and domains. The multiple contour assessment framework represents an innovative and groundbreaking concept that has never been applied to the evaluation of computer-based models prior to our proposed method. The extension of this concept to three-dimensional data and the integration of time as a key variable in the analysis represents an advanced and sophisticated approach that has never been previously reported. We explore the effect of liquid slip on the dynamics of a liquid droplet forming on a fiber, combining molecular dynamics simulations with experimental findings. At certain conditions, the presence of slip leads to larger droplet sizes, opposing the typically observed reduction due to liquid slip. Additionally, large enough slips cause the liquid to accumulate at the fiber's ends, preventing the breakup of the fiber and altering the dynamics significantly. A theoretical model incorporating these effects accurately predicts the observed change in droplet size. These cross-scale simulations provide insight into the role of liquid slip in fluid dynamics and offer explanations for earlier experiments. Furthermore, these results suggest the feasibility of manipulating droplet formation via slip by employing tailored surfaces, opening doors for applications in biotechnology and microfluidics. A test for the accuracy of SFR measurements revealed that these rates are subject to random variability and are typically within a 0.1-0.3 M$_{\odot$yr$^{-1}$ range. Consequently, the use of this efficiency in further studies may be inappropriate. In contrast, the star formation rates derived through Sed fitting are found to be a reliable and effective metric for the investigation of various galaxy types. Comprised of multiple sub-models, spHabitat offers a versatile solution for a broad range of spatial ecology challenges. The package features sub-routines for habitat selection, growth, migration, interaction, and collision, along with re-implementation of the State-space Habitat Relationship (SHR) model and an enhanced multi-species spatial recreation model derived from Bovay and Lebreton (2009). Additionally, spHabitat includes sub-routines for single-species spatial ecology applications, such as re-implementation of the spatial population growth model (Pacilly et al., 2011) and an original migration model. The package also offers a general tool for spatial ecology applications, such as re-implementation of the spatial autocorrelation model (Augustin et al., 2009) and an original habitat selection model. The spHabitat software package is available for free download on the following website: http://sphabitat.free-blog.net/ spHabitat also includes a demo application showing its use in an example case to analyze the spatial distribution and habitat selection of the gray seal in Brittany, France. Deep multimodal learning using K-fan-based deep learning (KL) has gained significant advancements recently. Despite improvements, several fundamental challenges persist with existing multimodal deep learning models, including (1) the lack of a unified theoretical framework for deep multimodal learning, (2) the limited ability of models to learn and represent complex data, and (3) the difficulty in evaluating classification performance efficiently. A new K-fan deep learning model is proposed to address these challenges by providing a unified theoretical framework for deep multimodal learning. It learns shared representations using a shared hidden layer with optimized weights, and has multiple independent output layers with unique weights for each modality. Additionally, the model incorporates feature learning, shared representations, and a low-rank multi-modal learning component to learn unbalanced multimodal data efficiently. A new learning algorithm for the model, L1-KL, is also developed based on the model's unique hidden layer with the L1-norm constraint. Experimental evaluations of the model demonstrate its effectiveness on 29 balanced datasets and 13 unbalanced datasets across various classification tasks. It achieved superior or comparable performance compared to 30 prominent deep multimodal learning models, and required significantly reduced computational resources, evaluating classification performance using only a small subset of data instead of the entire dataset. The model's performance is remarkable, and it has surpassed many deep multimodal learning models even with evaluation classification performance optimization. The study also validated the model's efficacy on open-access dataset collections and real-world application datasets, and provided comprehensive analysis of the model's performance and its implications on deep multimodal learning research. A dataset with detailed information on the model and its evaluation is available for public access at https://github.com/alimomoh/K-fan_MM_Learning. L1-KL is an extendable deep multimodal learning model, and the study's findings can be generalized to other deep multimodal learning models using K-fan deep learning. The model's unique hidden layer with the L1-norm constraint can be integrated into existing deep multimodal learning models to improve their performance and efficiency. The study offers a new perspective on deep multimodal learning based on K-fan deep learning, and can be applied to other areas of machine learning and pattern analysis. The global pandemic has underscored the critical role social media plays in disseminating information. As a result, there has been a surge in malicious misinformation spread via social media, which poses significant public health risks. Given the concentric nature of social media networks, where inner groups tend to share content more widely with one another, we observed a notable phenomenon in WhatsApp groups during the early stages of the pandemic in Brazil. This led us to develop a computational framework that quantifies the risk of malicious misinformation within WhatsApp groups before it spreads to outer groups. Based on this, we propose a straightforward strategy for WhatsApp to combat misinformation: close private groups to new members. Our analysis reveals that this approach can significantly reduce the likelihood of malicious misinformation spreading, thus protecting less informed group members from misinformation exposure. Furthermore, we discovered similar effects on public WhatsApp groups in Brazil and India, as well as comparable outcomes on other social media platforms such as Telegram. Ultimately, our findings position WhatsApp as a key player in combating misinformation within its platform, while also advocating for multi-faceted efforts against misinformation that take into account the complexities and limitations of social media networks. To combat spoofing attacks on speech-based systems, a novel approach called SpoofingCountering (SC) is utilized. SC systems reevaluate the authenticity of speech in real-time by incorporating speech characteristics that are difficult for impersonators to replicate. However, the effectiveness of these systems can be hindered by their minimal capacity to learn complex features and inherent difficulties in adapting to various attack types. A prominent drawback of existing SC methods is their inability to effectively utilize the unique characteristics extracted and concentrate their attention on relevant high-level speech features. A novel mechanism called Attentive Activation (AA) is proposed to overcome these limitations. AA acts as an enhanced activation function for improving the performance of SC networks by selectively amplifying key speech features and emphasizing the authenticity confidence. This approach is comprised of two main components: the conventional ReLU and a self-designed attention module. During the backward pass, AA identifies and amplifies prominent features while suppressing insignificant ones, thereby preventing unnecessary information flow. Furthermore, AA incorporates an attention mechanism that calculates a weighted average of input neuron activations based on their significance. Experimental results on the NIST2019 LFCC dataset have demonstrated the superiority of the proposed AA mechanism over traditional SC networks and other alternative activation functions. The ultimate goal is to develop an SC system that can adapt to multiple attack types and leverage low-level speech characteristics effectively. The proposed AA mechanism has shown the potential to enhance the performance of end-to-end spoofing counteraction systems, which are to be continuously updated in the future. The code for this research can be found at: https://github.com/ozanovoz/AttentiveActivation. The amount of asymmetry in photon pair formation when one photon is detected can be calculated using the linear dichroic ratio. This calculation assumes a linear polarization model and involves estimating two unknown angles based on measurable quantities. Ultimately, the linear dichroic ratio provides information about the direction of photon pair formation and allows us to describe its angular dependence. Modern network defense tools rely heavily on adaptive protocols to communicate securely. Yet, their source code is freely available, posing significant risks, as an adversary can study the code and develop effective exploitation techniques. This has led researchers to investigate the feasibility of identifying these tools using dynamic traffic patterns. Surprisingly, the results show that without initial knowledge of the tool, identification is highly impossible or extremely difficult in certain situations. This research delivers the first comprehensive assessment of deep learning-based classification methods for adaptive protocol users. Contrary to existing positive findings, our study reveals that an adversary can easily thwart these classification methods using previously unknown attacks. Specifically, we demonstrate that sequence-based models can be successfully deceived by generating intricate payloads that manipulate traffic sequences. Moreover, the same payload can be used across multiple types of networks, while also evading detection by appearing legitimate. Notably, this research showcases that an adaptive protocol tool can be compromised simply by modifying its source code. This threatens not just individual tools but also the entire category of network defense tools. An adversary can exploit this by creating a "supervised" training environment, where they simulate various types of networks and data flows, before using previously discovered vulnerabilities to develop novel exploits. This yields highly realistic, multi-type network FPs. This research also proposes an alternative method where an adversary can evade deep learning-based F-D DET without making any changes to the tool's source code. Specifically, our results show that fine-tuning alone can render a trained model ineffective. This research also underscores the need for constant monitoring of network defense tools due to the inherent instability and lack of reliability of their adaptive protocols. Constant validation by means of deep learning is also necessary since the mere periodic updating of these tools proves inadequate. Ultimately, our research implies that purely open-source tools should not be relied upon for critical network defense missions due to the unacceptably high risks involved. This research is intended to be a starting point for further study in this area, promoting a more nuanced understanding of the complex trade-offs inherent in using adaptive protocol tools. Additionally, we outline potential future research avenues at the end of the paper. Specifically, we suggest investigating the possibility of training models without source code access through self-supervised or semi-supervised learning approaches. Moreover, we ponder whether the inherent instability of adaptive protocols could be deliberately leveraged to develop an unrecognizable or unidentifiable network defense asset. Lastly, we raise the possibility that the mere presence of deep learning-based classification has an adverse effect on the security of adaptive protocol tools, thereby potentially creating a backdoor effect

To optimize the performance of the individual users and the entire system, a comprehensive mathematical model is developed and analyzed. Subsequently, an advanced estimation method, known as cascaded channel estimation (CCE), is proposed to minimize operational complexity. Notably, the CCE technique offers the ability to utilize the reflected signals from previous users to facilitate channel estimation for subsequent users. As such, the proposed CCE method yields substantial improvements in operational efficiency, ultimately resulting in a "greater-than-sum" effect. Furthermore, the proposed CCE technique is quantitatively evaluated using two specific scenarios: a multi-user MISO system with multiple reflectarrays and a virtual MISO system with multiple reflectarrays. Additionally, the Simulink graphics depicted in this research showcase the efficient channel estimation capability of the proposed CCE technique. This study analyzes data from multiple sources for 93 U.S. regions, examining relationships between COVID-coverage in regional news outlets, infection rates, fatality rates, and audience size. A large dataset of television news transcripts, totaling 879,016 entries from 82 outlets, is utilized to measure COVID-related coverage in 93 regions over a 25-month period. A combination of natural language processing and machine learning enables the identification of coverage duration, along with the correlates of regional news coverage, despite potential biases. Structural equation models indicate that regional news outlets influence public awareness, and their coverage duration has a direct impact on infection and death rates. Furthermore, factors such as population size, demographics, and news outlet audience size are found to influence regional news coverage duration. A 1-month increase in COVID coverage in regional news is associated with a 1.1% increase in daily COVID deaths and a 0.7% increase in daily infection cases. These findings are consistent across different populations and demonstrate that regional news coverage has a positive correlation with COVID death rates and infection cases. A 1% increase in population size is associated with a 0.1% decrease in infection cases and a 0.4% decrease in death rates. A 1% increase in COVID coverage is associated with a 0.07% decrease in infection cases and a 0.06% decrease in death rates. Conversely, population demographics and audience size have no significant effect on infection and death rates. COVID-related coverage in regional news has a positive correlation with infection and death rates, and its impact may be attributed to increased public awareness, leading to more frequent testing and reporting of cases and deaths. These findings have implications for understanding the influence of media coverage and are of particular relevance during public health crises, where accurate and transparent communication to the public can help mitigate the spread of diseases. A new class of advanced keys-only filters called Xor Filters is introduced, offering a more compact and efficient alternative to Bloom and Cuckoo filters. Essentially, each element in a hash table corresponds to a modded hash value, and any given element is included in the table if and only if the resulting value is zero when combined (using XOR operation) with its corresponding table entry. When it comes to inserting new elements, simply take the modded hash value, and place it in the corresponding index. Conversely, when encountering a query element, perform the XOR operation with each entry in the table; if the result is zero, the query element corresponds to a present item. Notably, due to the properties of XOR, only one bit per slot is required to keep track of used entries. Furthermore, when dealing with random hash functions, the expected density of used entries in a table of n entries is approximately k/n. As such, higher filter performance can be achieved by increasing the size of the table while maintaining the same number of entries. Moreover, the space savings can reach 33% improvement over the previously most efficient solutions (Bloom Filters). Regarding wrong positives, the expected count is approximately 2.5k/n, and this rate is nearly the best achievable as well. Ultimately, Xor Filters offers the smallest and most efficient keys-only filtering solution, boasting compact and efficient properties. An experimental evaluation of Xor Filters is also conducted, comparing its performance to other advanced filter solutions such as Cuckoo Filters, Chained Hash Filters, and Bloom Filters. Notably, Xor Filters outperforms the other solutions in almost all cases. As such, Xor Filters appears to be an excellent choice for use in statistics sampling, synchronization, distributed database querying, and other data processing applications. New code has been developed in C using the Silicon Avenue Chained Hash Filter and Cuckoo Filter libraries for comparison purposes. As such, Xor Filters can be easily implemented by incorporating the introduced modded hash and compact filtering techniques into existing filter software. In the near future, the authors plan to introduce more advanced features to further enhance the filtering capabilities. Possible future directions may involve incorporating support for non-binary hash functions, integrating sampling rates, or adding support for range-based queries. By leveraging the properties and efficiency of XOR operations, a more compact and efficient advanced keys-only filter class, Xor Filters, can be developed with a unique modded hash value mechanism and enhanced properties, including higher filter performance, reduced space usage, and lower wrong positive rates

This work presents FLVoogd, a robust federated learning framework capable of withstanding strategic and habitual malfeasance from participating nodes while preserving their individual data privacy. Specifically, we address the challenges of hiding collective model updates and shielding query results from malicious intermediaries. Our framework comprises two primary components: updates encrypted using various methods and a prototype based on zero-shot learning. Furthermore, we evaluate the effectiveness of integrating privacy-enhancing technologies, such as homomorphic encryption and secret sharing, into our framework. Experimental results validated the superiority of our framework in maintaining model performance and privacy under the threat of malicious interference. Additionally, we found that integrating privacy-enhancing technologies comes with a significant computational cost but offers notably improved resilience to malicious activities. Consequently, we provide recommendations for a suitable combination of techniques tailored to diverse use cases. A key obstacle in developing fully autonomous vehicles on a budget is overcoming the disparity between simulated and real-world environments. To address this issue, our approach is centered on creating an autonomous navigation system that learns in both domains simultaneously. By employing a novel task assignment method that utilizes image gradients, we enable the system to adapt to real-world scenarios while utilizing simulated data for optimization. The algorithm's performance was tested and evaluated on an F1 car using a modified AutoPS tool, yielding notable gains in lap times and a mean absolute error reduction of 27%. Furthermore, our method successfully mitigated the sim2real challenge, achieving results that outperformed existing solutions by a significant 11 seconds per lap. The associated code and simulation data can be accessed through our GitHub repository. Additionally, a video demonstration is available on YouTube. The simulation environment was developed in Unreal Engine 4 using our custom 'F1GameWorld' package. This engine was previously utilized in the renowned Formula 1 Game Series. Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of professional-grade deepfakes with minimal human input, thanks to advancements in techniques such as deep learning-based generative networks and unsupervised learning methods like GANs. This has raised serious concerns about the potential misuse of deepfakes in spreading false information. Despite focus on high-resolution video deepfakes, research on manipulating various media formats remains underrepresented. Consequently, there is an underdeveloped understanding of how to effectively detect such forms of media. In this study, we devise novel approaches to generate deepfakes seamlessly within common video content. To overcome detection challenges, we also develop a powerful, simple, and adaptable deepfake detection model based on multi-task learning. This framework serves as a robust benchmark for evaluating deepfake detection methods across diverse media content and demonstrates superior performance in this domain. To facilitate further research, we also establish a comprehensive deepfake dataset comprising various media types, which is accessible through our established website. This dataset significantly differs from existing ones as it covers a broader range of content types. This research contribution addresses multiple unsolved problems, such as detecting deepfakes presented as lip-synced audio clips or mixed into common images and videos. Moreover, we devise a multi-language deepfake detection model that focuses exclusively on speech. This work has the potential to expand the understanding and techniques for detecting deepfakes across all types of media formats. It also provides a broader research framework that can be applied beyond deepfake manipulation, encompassing manipulation of other media formats as well. The proposed methods and the newly created dataset will be made available for the research community. Additionally, an implementation of our deepfake detection model is also included in our research contribution. This allows for easier integration into other research projects and has the potential to advance future studies in this domain. Ultimately, this research addresses the critical underrepresented areas in deepfake research and presents a comprehensive deepfake dataset that can be employed in various content types to facilitate further research.
